data.rule: RFC 8785 Section 3.2.2.3; number serialization follows ECMAScript JSON.stringify/Number serialization, for which negative zero serializes as 0.
data.divergence_trap: An implementation that preserves the lexical token may emit {"n":-0}, which is not canonical JCS.

data.rule: RFC 8785 Section 3.2.2.3; numbers are serialized as ECMAScript IEEE-754 doubles. 2^53 is exactly representable.
data.divergence_trap: None for a conforming ECMAScript Number serializer; an arbitrary-precision JSON-number implementation may incorrectly preserve a different numeric model.

data.rule: RFC 8785 Section 3.2.2.3; parsing into an IEEE-754 binary64 number and subsequent ECMAScript serialization rounds 9007199254740993 to the representable value 9007199254740992.
data.divergence_trap: Arbitrary-precision JSON parsers that retain the decimal integer exactly may incorrectly emit 9007199254740993 rather than the JCS/ECMAScript Number result.

data.rule: RFC 8785 Section 3.2.2.3; ECMAScript uses fixed-point notation in this magnitude range, including 10^20.
data.divergence_trap: A serializer that always prefers exponent notation may emit {"n":1e+20}, which is not the canonical ECMAScript/JCS representation.

data.rule: RFC 8785 Section 3.2.2.3; ECMAScript switches to exponential notation at 10^21.
data.divergence_trap: A fixed-decimal serializer may emit {"n":1000000000000000000000}; a non-ECMAScript exponent formatter may emit 1E21 instead of the required lowercase e and explicit plus sign.

data.rule: RFC 8785 Section 3.2.2.3; ECMAScript uses fixed notation at 10^-6.
data.divergence_trap: A serializer that always uses scientific notation may emit {"n":1e-6}, which is not the canonical JCS representation.

data.rule: RFC 8785 Section 3.2.2.3; ECMAScript switches to exponential notation below 10^-6.
data.divergence_trap: A fixed-decimal serializer may emit {"n":0.0000001}; a naive scientific formatter may use 1E-7 rather than the required lowercase e and no unnecessary zero padding.

data.rule: RFC 8785 Section 3.2.2.2; only the required JSON escapes are used, and the solidus U+002F need not and does not get escaped. Reverse solidus and quotation mark are escaped; control characters use their short escapes where defined.
data.divergence_trap: A serializer that habitually escapes / may emit "\\/", producing different bytes. A serializer that uses non-canonical forms for control characters can also diverge.

data.rule: RFC 8785 Sections 3.2.2.2 and 3.2.3; JCS performs no Unicode normalization, while strings are serialized from Unicode values. A valid surrogate pair represents the corresponding non-BMP Unicode scalar value.
data.divergence_trap: A Unicode-normalizing implementation may incorrectly make the first two string values identical in representation. An implementation that preserves literal surrogate-pair escape spelling instead of serializing the Unicode character can diverge.

data.rule: RFC 8785 Section 3.2.3; object property names are sorted by their UTF-16 code-unit sequences, not by Unicode code-point order. U+10000 is encoded as D800 DC00, so it sorts before U+E000.
data.divergence_trap: A naive implementation that sorts decoded Unicode strings by code point can order U+E000 before U+10000 and emit {"":1,"𐀀":2}.

data.rule: RFC 8785 Sections 3.2.1 and 3.2.3; empty arrays/objects serialize as [] and {}, while object member names are recursively sorted using UTF-16 ordering.
data.divergence_trap: An implementation that sorts only the outermost object can leave the nested members as {"b":[],"a":1}, producing non-canonical output.

data.rule: RFC 8785 Section 3.1 and the JCS uniqueness requirement: object property names must be unique. Duplicate member names make the input unsuitable for deterministic JCS canonicalization.
data.divergence_trap: A parser using last-wins semantics may silently reduce the input to {"a":2}; a first-wins parser may reduce it to {"a":1}. Both discard the fact that the original JSON had duplicate names.

receipt_kinds.when_produced: The non-succinct zkVM receipt produced directly from execution/segment proofs; it retains the composite/segment-level proof structure rather than reducing the proof to one recursive receipt.
A recursively compressed receipt in which the underlying composite execution proof has been reduced to a succinct proof. This is the intermediate proof form used by the recursion system.
A succinct receipt wrapped by the RISC Zero Groth16 recursion circuit, producing a BN254 Groth16 proof ('seal') that can be verified with a Groth16 verifying key.

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: ReceiptClaim (version-dependent internal shape; conceptually pre-state, post-state, exit code, input digest, output/journal digest)
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: The statement certified by the receipt. The journal bytes are not themselves the Groth16 claim field; the claim commits to the execution result including the journal/output digest and the execution state transition.
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Recompute the claim digest from the canonical ReceiptClaim representation and use that digest as the expected Groth16 public input. Also validate the semantic relationship between the claim and the requested image ID and journal.
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: An attacker could pair a valid Groth16 proof for one execution claim with a different claim object supplied to the verifier, causing the verifier to accept a valid proof as certification of a different program/result.

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: byte string containing the Groth16 proof over BN254; exact serialized length/encoding is circuit/library-version dependent
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: The actual Groth16 proof produced by the RISC Zero Groth16 wrapping circuit.
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Parse the proof using the exact RISC Zero Groth16 encoding rules, verify it with the correct circuit-specific verifying key, and supply the exact expected public inputs, including the claim digest and the circuit/control-root commitment required by that version.
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: If the seal is not cryptographically verified, an attacker can submit arbitrary or unrelated claim data without possessing a proof of execution.

components.meaning: The initial VM/system state commitment. In RISC Zero versions where ReceiptClaim exposes SystemState, this is a structured state commitment rather than simply a field literally named image_id. The program image identity is bound through the initial machine state/commitment used by the VM.
The final VM/system state commitment resulting from execution.
The VM execution outcome/status. A verifier requiring successful execution must enforce the appropriate success exit code rather than merely checking that a proof exists.
Digest/commitment to the committed execution input.
Digest/commitment to the execution output, which is the commitment used to bind the journal contents in the receipt API.

claim_structure.image_id: The image ID is not safely described across all v1.x-3.x releases as a direct ReceiptClaim field named image_id. The important invariant is that the claim's initial state commitment is bound to the executable image identity, and verification against a caller-supplied image ID must enforce that binding.
claim_structure.journal_digest: The receipt carries journal bytes separately from the cryptographic claim. The claim contains the corresponding output/journal commitment; verification of a supplied journal therefore requires recomputing the canonical journal/output digest and checking equality with the claim.
claim_structure.claim_digest: The Groth16 statement is not formed by hashing an arbitrary JSON serialization. RISC Zero defines a canonical ReceiptClaim digest routine in its zkVM receipt implementation. Mechanically, the verifier must compute exactly the protocol-defined digest over the canonical encoded claim fields and use that resulting 32-byte Digest as the corresponding Groth16 public input. Exact serialization/hash framing is implementation-version specific and should be taken from the matching risc0-zkvm source rather than reimplemented from a generic serialization scheme.

binding_chain.detail: The journal bytes are committed by the receipt's output/journal digest. A verifier that exposes journal bytes to an application must recompute the protocol-defined digest from those bytes and compare it with the digest committed by the claim.
The ReceiptClaim's canonical fields are encoded according to the RISC Zero receipt implementation and passed through its claim-digest routine. This produces the digest representing the exact claim.

The Groth16 circuit proves a statement whose public inputs include the claim digest. Therefore the Groth16 proof is bound to that exact claim rather than merely to an unstructured receipt byte string.

binding_chain.binding: control-root/circuit commitment -> Groth16 public input and circuit
binding_chain.detail: The RISC Zero Groth16 wrapper is tied to the recursion circuit configuration and its control commitment/root. The verifier must use the expected control-root value for the intended RISC Zero version/configuration and the matching Groth16 verifying key.

The Groth16 seal is verified against the circuit-specific BN254 verifying key. Successful verification therefore establishes that the supplied public inputs satisfy the RISC Zero Groth16 wrapping circuit.

The complete application-level check is consequently: the requested image/program identity is the one bound by the claim's initial state, the supplied journal hashes to the claim's output/journal commitment, the claim digest is recomputed exactly, the Groth16 proof verifies against the exact expected public inputs/control commitment, and the exit code satisfies the policy being requested.

version_coupling.verifying_key: Circuit/version dependent. A Groth16 verifying key is tied to a particular Groth16 circuit. Using a key for a different RISC Zero circuit/version is not a harmless substitution: a legitimate seal from the intended circuit will generally fail verification, while accepting a key for an unintended circuit can destroy the verifier's intended statement if the surrounding checks are not correspondingly updated.
version_coupling.control_root: Version/circuit dependent. The control root represents the approved recursion-control configuration for the relevant proof system/version. It must match the expected root for the circuit and receipt ecosystem being verified.
version_coupling.control_ids: The underlying recursion control IDs and their Merkle/root commitment are also version/configuration sensitive. They should not be treated as stable constants across risc0-zkvm releases.
version_coupling.claim_encoding: The exact canonical encoding and claim-digest construction are implementation details that can change with receipt/circuit revisions. A verifier should use the matching risc0-zkvm implementation rather than assuming that the v1.x encoding is identical to v2.x or v3.x.
version_coupling.failure_mode: Using the wrong version's parameters normally causes valid proofs to fail because the seal, verifying key, public-input interpretation, or control commitment no longer matches. A more dangerous implementation mistake is to mix parameters from different versions while omitting an explicit version/circuit binding; this can create cross-version confusion about what exactly was proven.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Checks the Groth16 seal but does not recompute the claim digest from the supplied claim.
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches_it: Recompute ReceiptClaim::digest() (or the exact equivalent for the selected risc0-zkvm version) and compare the resulting digest with the Groth16 public input used for verification.
common_verifier_bugs.concrete_failure: A proof for claim A could be presented alongside attacker-controlled claim B, and the verifier could accidentally report that B was proven.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Accepts journal bytes without checking that they hash to the claim's output/journal digest.
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches_it: Recompute the protocol-defined journal/output digest over the exact journal bytes and compare it to the digest committed in the claim.
common_verifier_bugs.concrete_failure: A valid proof for journal J1 could be accompanied by forged journal bytes J2, causing an application to consume data that was never proven.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Fails to bind the receipt to the requested image ID/program identity.
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches_it: Validate the claim's initial state/image binding against the exact expected image ID using the risc0-zkvm verification logic for the relevant release.
common_verifier_bugs.concrete_failure: A receipt proving a different executable could be accepted as proof of the caller's intended program.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Uses the wrong Groth16 verifying key or accepts a caller-selected key without separately binding it to the intended RISC Zero circuit/version.
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches_it: Select the verifying key from trusted, version-specific parameters and verify the seal with that exact key.
common_verifier_bugs.concrete_failure: The verifier could accept a proof generated for a different circuit/protocol configuration and mistake it for a proof of the intended RISC Zero statement.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Does not enforce the expected control root/control-ID commitment.
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches_it: Compare the control commitment/public input against the trusted expected value for the exact circuit/version before accepting the Groth16 proof.
common_verifier_bugs.concrete_failure: A mathematically valid Groth16 proof from a different recursion-control configuration could be accepted as though it certified the intended RISC Zero recursion system.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Treats 'proof verifies' as equivalent to 'successful program execution' without checking the exit code.
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches_it: Enforce the expected successful ExitCode, or explicitly propagate failure semantics to the caller.
common_verifier_bugs.concrete_failure: A receipt proving a program that deterministically halted with a failure/panic exit could be mistakenly treated as proof of successful execution.

certainty_notes.receipt_kinds: High confidence on the composite/succinct/groth16 progression and their roles. Exact construction paths/default APIs can differ across risc0-zkvm releases.
certainty_notes.groth16_receipt_fields: High confidence that the Groth16 receipt conceptually consists of a ReceiptClaim plus Groth16 seal/proof. Exact Rust field names and wrapper types should be checked against the target release because RISC Zero changed receipt APIs and serialization across versions.
certainty_notes.claim_structure: Moderate-to-high confidence on the conceptual fields: pre-state, post-state, exit code, input digest, and output/journal digest. I am deliberately not asserting that every v1.x-3.x release exposed an image_id field literally by that name, because the image identity is represented through the initial system-state commitment in relevant receipt designs.
certainty_notes.claim_digest: High confidence that verification must use the RISC Zero-defined canonical claim-digest procedure and must not substitute arbitrary serialization. Lower confidence in a byte-for-byte reconstruction of every version's internal encoding from memory alone; this is precisely the part that should be taken from the matching risc0-zkvm source before implementing an independent verifier.
certainty_notes.binding_chain: High confidence in the cryptographic dependency chain: journal/output commitment -> claim -> claim digest -> Groth16 public input -> Groth16 seal verification, with program/image identity and recursion-control configuration also bound into the statement.
certainty_notes.version_coupling: High confidence that Groth16 verifying keys, recursion control commitments/IDs, and circuit parameters are version/configuration coupled. Exact parameter names and packaging vary by release.
certainty_notes.common_verifier_bugs: These are concrete, standard failure modes for a RISC Zero-style receipt verifier; the exact method names used to prevent them are version dependent.
certainty_notes.source_scope: The attached document specifies that the requested target is the RISC Zero receipt format, especially the Groth16-wrapped form, and explicitly requires version sensitivity and per-section honesty notes.

receipt_kinds.description: A receipt made up of one receipt for every segment in a zkVM execution, and every assumption. Size is linear with respect to execution length. Produced when `ReceiptKind::Composite` is requested. Useful for development and debugging, but not for production due to size.

A receipt where all segments have been compressed into a single STARK proof. Size is constant with respect to execution length. Produced when `ReceiptKind::Succinct` is requested. This is an intermediate step, often used before further compression to Groth16.

A receipt composed of a Groth16 proof over the BN254 curve. It is the smallest and most compact receipt format, constant in size, and can be serialized to a few hundred bytes. Produced when `ReceiptKind::Groth16` is requested. This is the format intended for on-chain verification and production use.
receipt_kinds.produced_when: Requested via `Prover::prove_with_opts` with `ReceiptKind::Groth16`. Also produced by compressing a `SuccinctReceipt` using a Groth16 prover.

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: Vec<u8>
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: The raw Groth16 proof data, serialized as a byte vector. It contains the cryptographic proof that attests to the validity of the `ReceiptClaim`.
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: The verifier must deserialize this seal, extract the Groth16 proof components (a, b, c), and verify it against the public inputs derived from the `ReceiptClaim` and the `VerifierContext` (which contains the verifying key and control root). The verification process is invoked via `verify_integrity()` or `verify_integrity_with_context()`.
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: If the verifier ignores the `seal`, the proof is not cryptographically checked. An attacker could trivially forge a receipt by constructing a fake `ReceiptClaim` with any desired journal and image ID, as there is no cryptographic binding.

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: MaybePruned<Claim> where Claim: Digestible + Debug + Clone + Serialize
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: The `ReceiptClaim` which contains the public outputs of the execution: the image ID (program identifier), the journal digest, the exit code, and any assumptions. It may be pruned to reduce size, but the digest of the claim is always available.
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: The verifier must compute the digest of the `ReceiptClaim` (via `claim.digest()`) and use it as part of the public inputs to the Groth16 verifier. After cryptographic verification, the verifier should check that the claimed image ID matches the expected program, the exit code is successful (e.g. `Halted(0)`), and the journal digest matches the hash of the provided journal bytes.
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: If the verifier does not use the claim digest in the public inputs, the seal is not bound to the claim. An attacker could present a valid seal from one execution (e.g., with a benign image ID) and pair it with a different claim (e.g., with a malicious image ID), and the verification would pass.

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: Digest (a 32-byte hash)
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: A digest (fingerprint) of the verifier parameters that must be used to verify this receipt. This includes the Groth16 verifying key and the control IDs that commit to the RISC Zero circuits. It acts as a version identifier for the proof system and circuits.
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: The verifier must ensure that the `verifier_parameters` digest matches the digest of the `VerifierContext` (or the specific `Groth16ReceiptVerifierParameters`) it intends to use. If they do not match, verification must fail. This prevents using a receipt generated with one version of the zkVM or one set of circuits with a different verifier.
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: If the verifier ignores `verifier_parameters`, it might use the wrong verifying key. An attacker could generate a receipt using an older, vulnerable version of the zkVM (or a custom circuit) and present it to a verifier expecting a newer, secure version, potentially bypassing security fixes or exploiting known vulnerabilities in the older version.

components.name: pre
components.description: The image ID (a `Digest`) of the guest program that was executed. This is the hash of the program's ELF file and uniquely identifies the code.

components.name: output
components.description: The public output of the execution, which includes the journal (public data written by the guest) and any assumptions (proof composition requirements).

components.name: journal
components.description: The public output bytes written by the guest program. The `ReceiptClaim` contains a `Digest` of these bytes (the `journalDigest`).

components.name: assumptions
components.description: A list of claims that were verified inside the guest using `env::verify()`. These are resolved during proof composition. The `ReceiptClaim` can contain unresolved assumptions, which are then proven by additional receipts.

components.name: exit_code
components.description: The exit status of the guest program, e.g., `Halted(0)` for a successful execution.

claim_structure.claim_digest_computation: The `ReceiptClaim` implements the `Digestible` trait. The digest is computed by hashing the serialized components of the claim (pre, journal_digest, exit_code, assumptions, etc.) using the Poseidon2 hash function (in newer versions) or Poseidon (in older versions). This digest is the `claim_digest` that is used as a public input to the Groth16 proof.

steps.description: Journal bytes → Journal Digest. The verifier computes the SHA-256 digest of the provided journal bytes.

Journal Digest + Image ID + Exit Code + Assumptions → ReceiptClaim Digest. The verifier reconstructs the `ReceiptClaim` from these components (or receives it directly) and computes its digest (using Poseidon2).

ReceiptClaim Digest → Groth16 Public Inputs. The claim digest is split into two field elements (`c0`, `c1`) and used as public inputs to the Groth16 verifier, along with the control root (`a0`, `a1`) from the `VerifierContext`.

Groth16 Public Inputs + Seal → Verification. The Groth16 verifier checks the proof (`seal`) against the public inputs and the verifying key (from the `VerifierContext`). The `verifier_parameters` digest ensures the correct verifying key and control root are used.

binding_chain.where_control_root_and_vk_enter: The `VerifierContext` (or `Groth16ReceiptVerifierParameters`) provides the Groth16 verifying key and the `control_root`. The `control_root` is split into two field elements (`a0`, `a1`) and is included in the public inputs. This binds the proof to the specific RISC Zero circuits (the control root is a commitment to the STARK-to-SNARK wrapper). The verifying key is used by the Groth16 verifier to check the proof's validity.

components.description: The Groth16 verifying key is specific to the RISC Zero zkVM version and the specific circuit (e.g., the recursion circuit). It is embedded in the `VerifierContext`.
components.breaks_when_wrong_version: If the verifier uses a verifying key that does not match the one used to generate the proof, the Groth16 verification will fail. The `verifier_parameters` digest in the receipt is designed to catch this mismatch.

components.description: The control root is a commitment to the set of control IDs that define the RISC Zero zkVM circuits. It is part of the public inputs.
components.breaks_when_wrong_version: If the verifier uses a different control root than the one the proof was generated against, the public inputs will not match, and the Groth16 verification will fail. This ensures that the proof corresponds to the correct set of zkVM circuits (e.g., no malicious modifications). The `verifier_parameters` digest includes the control root, so a mismatch is caught early.

components.description: Older versions of the zkVM used Poseidon, while newer versions (v0.21.0+) use Poseidon2 for recursive proofs.
components.breaks_when_wrong_version: If a verifier expects one hash function but the receipt was generated with another, the digest computations (e.g., of the `ReceiptClaim`) will differ, causing the public inputs to mismatch and verification to fail. The `verifier_parameters` digest implicitly encodes this choice, preventing cross-version verification.

version_coupling.what_breaks: Using the wrong version's parameters (verifying key, control root, or hash function) will cause the Groth16 verification to fail. The `verifier_parameters` digest acts as a fingerprint to prevent this. In smart contract routers, a version mismatch results in a failure to find a registered verifier.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Ignoring the verifier_parameters digest and using a hardcoded verifying key.
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches_it: The verifier should compute the digest of its `VerifierContext` (or `Groth16ReceiptVerifierParameters`) and compare it to the `verifier_parameters` field in the receipt. If they do not match, verification must fail.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Failing to verify that the exit code is `Halted(0)` (successful execution).
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches_it: After cryptographic verification, the verifier must check the `exit_code` field of the `ReceiptClaim` to ensure the guest program completed successfully.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Not checking that the provided journal bytes hash to the `journalDigest` in the `ReceiptClaim`.
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches_it: The verifier must compute the SHA-256 digest of the provided journal bytes and compare it to the `journal_digest` in the `ReceiptClaim`.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Using the wrong field element ordering or splitting when constructing public inputs from the claim digest.
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches_it: The verifier must follow the exact specification for splitting the digest into field elements (e.g., `split_digest`). An incorrect split will cause the public inputs to be wrong, and the Groth16 verification will fail.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Failing to verify assumptions (proof composition) or treating them incorrectly.
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches_it: The verifier must ensure that all assumptions in the `ReceiptClaim` are resolved (i.e., there is a corresponding receipt for each assumption). This is typically handled by the `resolve` function, but a custom verifier must implement this logic.

certainty_notes.receipt_kinds: High confidence. Based on the `ReceiptKind` enum documentation and developer docs.
certainty_notes.groth16_receipt_fields: High confidence. Based on the `Groth16Receipt` struct definition from the source code.
certainty_notes.claim_structure: High confidence. Based on developer docs on proof composition and the `ReceiptClaim` definition. The exact set of fields may vary slightly between versions, but `image_id`, `journal_digest`, `exit_code`, and `assumptions` are core.
certainty_notes.binding_chain: High confidence. Based on the `verify_integrity_with_context` implementation, which splits the claim digest and control root for public inputs, and the documentation on how the journal digest is used.
certainty_notes.version_coupling: High confidence. Based on the documentation for `verifier_parameters`, the `VerifierContext`, and the version router contracts. The Poseidon/Poseidon2 change is noted in the release notes.
certainty_notes.common_verifier_bugs: High confidence. These are common errors in implementing zero-knowledge proof verifiers, derived from general security principles and specific RISC Zero documentation (e.g., the need to check exit code and journal digest).
certainty_notes.field_names: High confidence for the main fields (`seal`, `claim`, `verifier_parameters`). The `ReceiptClaim` fields (`pre`, `output`, `journal`, `assumptions`, `exit_code`) are based on the documentation and general knowledge of the system. Minor variations in naming across versions are possible, but the concepts are stable.

data.formula_basis: MAR33 / Parametric Normal ES: VaR_alpha(X) = mu + sigma * z_{1-alpha}; ES_alpha(X) = mu + sigma * [phi(z_{1-alpha}) / alpha], where alpha = 1 - 0.975 = 0.025.
data.weakest_point: Assumption of exact normality for trading P&L distributions, which typically exhibit fat tails in real market regimes.

data.case_name: Parametric ES at 99.0% under Standard Normality

inputs.risk_factor_category: Large cap equity price / FX major

data.formula_basis: MAR33.31 / MAR33.32: ES = sqrt(sum_{j} (ES_j(T_j) * sqrt((LH_j - LH_{j-1}) / 10))^2); for a single risk factor category with LH = 20 days, ES(20) = ES(10) * sqrt(20 / 10).
data.weakest_point: Square-root-of-time scaling assumes independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) returns across extended holding periods.

computation.tail_selection_rule_applied: Fractional observation tail convention: Top observation (k=1, Loss=150.0) weighted at 0.5 fraction relative to total alpha mass (0.5 / 0.5 = 1.0 weight). Alternative standard convention: ceiling(N * alpha) = 1 observation (Loss=150.0). Both conventions evaluate to the worst single observation for N=20.
computation.var_97_5_interpolation: Linear interpolation between rank 1 (150.0) and rank 2 (120.0) for 97.5th percentile (0.5th rank): 150.0

data.formula_basis: MAR33.3: ES_alpha = (1 / alpha) * integral_0^alpha VaR_u(X) du. Empirical discrete form: ES_alpha = (1 / (N * alpha)) * sum_{i=1}^floor(N*alpha) X_(i) + fractional remainder weighted accordingly.
data.weakest_point: Small sample discretization error: for N=20, 2.5% tail represents only 0.5 observations, causing ES to degenerate to the single worst sample loss.

data.vector_name: String escaping: Solidus and control character escaping
data.rule: RFC 8785 Section 3.2.2.2 (Strings) - Solidus '/' MUST NOT be escaped; control characters U+0000 through U+001F MUST be escaped using \u00XX or standard two-character escapes.

data.rule: RFC 8785 Section 3.2.2.2 (Strings) - Unicode characters MUST NOT be normalized (NFC/NFD transformations are explicitly forbidden).

data.vector_name: Key ordering: UTF-16 code-unit sort order vs Unicode code-point order
data.rule: RFC 8785 Section 3.2.3 (Object Keys) - Keys are sorted by UTF-16 code units. High surrogate U+D834 (0xD834) sorts BEFORE BMP character U+E000 (0xE000), even though code point U+1D11E > U+E000.
data.divergence_trap: Languages sorting keys by Unicode code points (e.g. Python string comparison) place U+E000 before U+1D11E, producing wrong key order.

data.rule: RFC 8785 Section 3.2.3 (Object Keys) - Keys MUST be sorted lexicographically by UTF-16 code unit values.
data.divergence_trap: JS engines that reorder numeric keys first based on integer property traversal order (e.g. key '1' then '10' then 'a' then 'b' in ES6 object iteration vs map).

receipt_kinds: CompositeReceipt: A receipt containing a vector of SegmentReceipts representing execution segments without recursive aggregation, produced directly by the prover when recursion is disabled or not requested.
SuccinctReceipt: A single STARK-based receipt produced by passing a segment or composite receipt through the recursive prover (lift/join/resolve) to aggregate execution into a single succinct proof.

Groth16Receipt: A compressed receipt produced by running the succinct STARK proof through the STARK-to-Groth16 recursion circuit, yielding a Groth16 proof over the BN254 curve suitable for low-cost on-chain verification (e.g. EVM).

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: Bytes / [u8; 256] or 8x U255/U256 group elements (a, b, c points on BN254)
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: The raw Groth16 cryptographic proof (pairing elements pi_a, pi_b, pi_c over BN254 curves).
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Perform the Groth16 pairing check e(a, b) = e(alpha, beta) + e(L, gamma) + e(c, delta) against the verifying key (vk) and public inputs.
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: Attacker can supply an arbitrary invalid seal byte array and forge verification without executing a valid zkVM trace.

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: ReceiptClaim struct (containing ImageID, PostState, ExitCode, Output/Journal Digest)
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: The statement of execution that the proof attests to, defining what program ran and what output was committed.
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Hash the claim into a claim digest (using Poseidon2 / SHA-256) and ensure it matches the public inputs encoded in the Groth16 proof/seal.
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: Attacker can swap the execution claim (e.g., replace ImageID with a malicious program or swap output journal) while reusing a valid proof for an unrelated claim.

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: Bytes (Vec<u8>)
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: The committed public output written by the guest program during execution via env::commit.
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Hash the journal bytes using SHA-256 and verify that SHA-256(journal) matches the journal digest specified inside the ReceiptClaim.
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: Attacker can replace public journal output bytes (e.g., alter recipient address or token amount) while keeping the original valid claim digest intact.

components.input_digest: Digest (32 bytes) of the initial input provided to the guest.
components.pre_state_digest: Digest (32 bytes) representing the initial image ID / Merkle root of the ELF memory before execution.
components.post_state_digest: Digest (32 bytes) representing the final execution state / Merkle root after guest halt.
components.output_digest: Digest (32 bytes) of the Output struct containing the journal digest and assumptions digest.
components.exit_code: Enum (e.g. Halted(u32), Paused(u32), SystemSplit) indicating guest termination condition.

claim_structure.claim_digest_computation: The ReceiptClaim digest is computed by serializing the claim components into field elements/words and hashing them using the STARK/Recursion hash function (Poseidon2 in v1.x+ or SHA-256 depending on recursion tier) in a canonical struct layout.

binding_chain.step_1: Guest program writes bytes to journal -> hashed via SHA-256 to yield journal_digest.
binding_chain.step_2: journal_digest is combined with assumptions_digest into Output struct -> hashed to yield output_digest.
binding_chain.step_3: output_digest + pre_state_digest (Image ID) + post_state_digest + exit_code + input_digest form the ReceiptClaim.
binding_chain.step_4: ReceiptClaim is canonically hashed to produce claim_digest.
binding_chain.step_5: claim_digest is combined with the control_root / control_id (identifying the valid recursion circuits) to construct the public inputs of the Groth16 circuit.
binding_chain.step_6: Public inputs (split into 32-byte field elements / 16-bit words suitable for BN254 scalar field) + VK + seal are verified via Groth16 pairing evaluation.

version_coupling.circuit_version_dependent_parts: Groth16 Verifying Key (vk), Recursion Control Root / Control IDs (identifying allowed STARK recursive circuits), Poseidon hash constants.
version_coupling.failure_on_version_mismatch: If a verifier uses a VK or Control Root from a different RISC Zero version (e.g. v0.18 vs v1.0), the public input transformation or pairing evaluation fails, rejecting valid proofs, or if a generic/dummy VK is used, allows forged proofs that satisfy an unconstrained circuit.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Failing to check journal digest against SHA-256(journal)
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches_it: Asserting sha256(receipt.journal) == receipt.claim.output.journal_digest.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Ignoring exit_code check and accepting non-Halted executions

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Truncating or improperly endian-swapping BN254 scalar field elements when converting claim digest to Groth16 public inputs

certainty_notes.receipt_kinds: High certainty: Composite, Succinct, and Groth16 receipt variants are fundamental to RISC Zero v0.18–v1.x architecture.
certainty_notes.groth16_receipt_fields: High certainty: Field breakdown (seal, claim, journal) matches canonical risc0 Rust SDK and EVM verifier interfaces.
certainty_notes.claim_structure: Medium-High certainty: Component names (pre/post state, exit code, output digest) match RISC Zero v1.x ReceiptClaim layout.
certainty_notes.binding_chain: High certainty: The cascade from journal bytes -> SHA-256 -> ReceiptClaim -> claim digest -> Groth16 public inputs is exact.
certainty_notes.version_coupling: High certainty: Control IDs and Groth16 VKs change per release and strictly govern recursion acceptance.
certainty_notes.common_verifier_bugs: High certainty: Standard attack vectors identified in zkVM verifier audits.

data.vector_name: RFC 8785 Appendix B extended test data (numbers, string, literals, whitespace)
data.rule: RFC 8785 Appendix B (extended test data, expected output as published); mechanics: §3.2.2.2 string escaping (short forms \b\t\n\f\r, remaining C0 as lowercase 4-hex, no solidus escape), §3.2.2.3 numbers via ES6 §7.1.12.1 shortest round-trip, §3.2.3 key sorting, no insignificant whitespace.
data.divergence_trap: Python json.dumps(sort_keys=True) escapes € as \u20ac (ensure_ascii default); literal-preserving serializers keep '4.50' and '1E30' verbatim instead of '4.5'/'1e+30'. JS JSON.stringify with sorted keys happens to match (JCS was modeled on it), which falsely reassures non-JS porters.

data.vector_name: Negative zero and zero with fraction
data.rule: §3.2.2.3: numbers are IEEE-754 doubles serialized per ES6 Number::toString; ±0 maps to '0', and integral values print without a fractional part.
data.divergence_trap: serde_json emits '-0.0' for -0.0; Python json.dumps(-0.0) → '-0.0'; Go emits '-0'; Python also emits '0.0' for 0.0 — all preserve the sign/dot the canonical form must drop.

data.rule: §3.1/§3.2.2.3: all input numbers are converted to IEEE-754 double before canonicalization. 9007199254740993 (2^53+1, odd) is not representable and rounds ties-to-even to 9007199254740992; 9007199254740994 is exactly representable.
data.divergence_trap: Any parser that preserves arbitrary precision — Python json.loads (int), Java BigDecimal, lossless-json — re-emits 9007199254740993 and the 'canonical' bytes differ from the double-conforming form.

data.rule: §3.2.2.3 via ES6 §7.1.12.1: fixed notation for 1e-6 ≤ |x| < 1e21, exponential for |x| ≥ 1e21; exponential form is lowercase 'e', carries '+', and has no zero-padded exponent digits.
data.divergence_trap: Python repr and Go strconv emit '1e+20' for 1e20 (they switch to exponential far below ES6's 1e21 threshold); C printf-style emitters pad exponents ('1e+021') or omit the '+' ('1e21').

data.rule: §3.2.2.3 via ES6 §7.1.12.1: |x| ≥ 1e-6 uses fixed notation ('0.000001'); |x| < 1e-6 switches to exponential with unpadded negative exponent ('1e-7').
data.divergence_trap: Python repr(1e-6)='1e-06' and repr(1e-7)='1e-07' (zero-padded two-digit exponent, wrong threshold); decimal-only formatters emit '0.0000001' for 1e-7.

data.rule: §3.2.2.3 via ES6 §7.1.12.1: output is the shortest string that round-trips the double — no trailing '.0', and the input's literal exponent form is never preserved.
data.divergence_trap: serde_json and Python emit '1.0' for 1.0; literal-preserving canonicalizers keep '1e2' or emit '100.0'.

data.vector_name: Control characters, short escapes, lowercase hex, and unescaped DEL
data.rule:
§3.2.2.2: only U+0000–U+001F, '"' and '\' are escaped;   	 
    use short forms, remaining C0 use lowercase 4-hex \u00xx; U+007F (DEL) is outside the escaped set and is emitted verbatim.
data.divergence_trap: Libraries that escape DEL ('\u007F') or emit uppercase hex ('\u001F', '\u000F') diverge; the canonical output's DEL is a raw 0x7F byte, and any uppercase-hex or DEL-escaping implementation fails byte comparison.

data.vector_name: Solidus, non-ASCII, and surrogate pair emitted verbatim
data.rule: §3.2.2.2: '/' (solidus) is NOT escaped; non-ASCII characters — including astral-plane characters represented by surrogate pairs — are emitted verbatim as UTF-8, never as \uXXXX.
data.divergence_trap: PHP json_encode (default flags) and ASP.NET JavaScriptSerializer emit '\/' for '/' and '\u20ac'/'\ud83d\ude00' escapes for the non-ASCII characters.

data.vector_name: UTF-16 code-unit ordering vs code-point ordering (astral vs U+E000–U+FFFF)
data.rule: §3.2.3: object members are sorted lexicographically by UTF-16 code unit values. '😀' = D83D DE00, 'ﬀ' = FB00, ' ' = FFFD; 0xD83D < 0xFB00 < 0xFFFD, so the astral key sorts FIRST even though its code point (U+1F600) is the largest.
data.divergence_trap: Code-point sorting (equivalently UTF-8 byte comparison, e.g. Python sorted(), Rust BTreeMap<&str>) yields ﬀ,  , 😀 — the astral key moves from first position to last; this is the classic JCS-vs-UTF-8-sorter divergence.

data.vector_name: No Unicode normalization: canonically equivalent keys stay distinct (U+03A9 omega vs U+2126 ohm sign)
data.rule: §3.2.2.2: strings are serialized verbatim — JCS applies NO Unicode normalization (NFC(U+2126) = U+03A9, but JCS must not perform it); §3.2.3 orders by UTF-16 units: 0x03A9 < 0x2126. First key is U+03A9 (Greek capital omega), second is U+2126 (ohm sign).
data.divergence_trap: An implementation that NFC-normalizes before serializing (a habit from RDF/JSON-LD canonicalization) merges the two canonically equivalent keys into a single member, changing both the key set and the byte output.

data.vector_name: Empty containers, nested structures, and array order preservation
data.rule: §3.2.3 sorts only object member names ('empty_arr' < 'empty_obj' < 'nested'; 'arr' < 'x'); arrays are ordered values and their element order MUST NOT be sorted; structures serialize compactly with no whitespace; empty containers are preserved.
data.divergence_trap: Pretty-printers inject spaces/newlines; over-eager canonicalizers sort array contents ([3,1,2] → [1,2,3]) or drop empty containers — both produce wrong canonical bytes.

data.vector_name: Duplicate object keys are illegal input
data.canonical_output: ERROR: duplicate member name 'a' — input rejected; JCS defines no canonical form for duplicate keys
data.rule: §3.1 (JCS input requirements: valid JSON with unique member names; canonicalization presupposes a one-to-one mapping) and Appendix B, which treats duplicate object keys as out-of-scope/undefined rather than defining a winner.
data.divergence_trap: JS JSON.parse silently keeps the last value ({"a":2}) while several other parsers keep the first ({"a":1}) — both emit a plausible-looking 'canonical' document, so signatures over either form are malleable and canonicalization-based checks can be bypassed; a conforming implementation must reject instead.

receipt_kinds.when_produced: Default Rust SDK output (no compression requested) in the 1.x era. Contains the per-segment STARK receipts for the whole session plus auxiliary receipts resolving execution assumptions (segment exit-code assumption and the po2/circuit-size assumption). Not recommended for third-party or on-chain verification because the recipient must re-verify the whole segment chain and assumption resolution. Field layout changed materially between 0.x (SegmentReceipt{index, po2, seal, hashfn}, no per-segment claim) and 1.x (segments carry claims/exit-code receipts); do not assume one shape across versions.
receipt_kinds.caveat: Exact CompositeReceipt field names (seal, assumption_receipts, exit_code_receipt, journal_digest/claim_digest) are 1.x-era and may have shifted in 2.x/3.x; I am least sure of this variant's exact struct.

receipt_kinds.when_produced: After running the risc0 recursion pipeline (lift/join/resolve over segments): a single STARK receipt whose circuit verifies the whole computation's final ReceiptClaim. Seal is a large Poseidon-based STARK proof; claim is a full ReceiptClaim; carries control ids (input/output control digests in 1.x, naming version-dependent) that the verifier must match against the control root of its trusted circuit set.

Compression of the Succinct receipt: the succinct STARK's verification is re-proven inside a Groth16 circuit over BN254 (circom-based stark-to-snark). Produced via risc0's groth16 prover when the user requests the compressed form; intended for cheap on-chain verification (Ethereum verifier contracts hardcode the Groth16 verifying key, control root, and bn254 control id). Introduced in the 1.0 line; does not exist in 0.x.

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: Raw Rust form: 256 bytes of Groth16 proof (pi_a G1 64B, pi_b G2 128B, pi_c G1 64B on BN254). ABI/Ethereum form: 592 bytes = 256B proof plus ~336B of receipt material (the serialized ReceiptClaim, 208B / 52 words, and the 4 public-input limbs: claim digest split into two 128-bit limbs + control root + bn254 control id, 128B). Exact ordering/offsets of the non-proof bytes vary by risc0-ethereum release; treat offsets as release-specific.
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: The cryptographic proof; everything else in the receipt is metadata the seal must commit to.
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Validate proof points are canonical (coordinates < field modulus, on-curve, correct subgroup, not point-at-infinity) before the pairing check; recompute the claim digest from the claim bytes carried in the seal (sha256 over the serialized claim) rather than trusting any digest field; check the recomputed digest equals the public-input limbs; check control root and bn254 control id equal the constants bound to the deployed verifying key; then run the pairing check.
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: If canonicality/on-curve checks are skipped, degenerate or malleated proofs (e.g., point-at-infinity or non-canonical coordinate encodings) can be crafted so a 'valid' seal exists without knowledge of a real proving key. If the claim digest is taken from a seal field instead of recomputed, an attacker swaps in a claim for a different program/exit code with the same journal digest and it passes.

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: ReceiptClaim: 52 words / 208 bytes in 1.x serialization (pre and post SystemState of 17 words each, 1-word exit code, 8-word input digest, 9-word optional output digest). In the Rust struct it embeds the journal for Groth16Receipt<Journal>; in the OuterReceipt the journal bytes sit outside.
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: The statement being proven: which program, what input, what final memory state, how it exited, and the journal commitment.
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Recompute sha256 over the serialized claim and compare to the public-input digest limbs; extract pre.digest (image ID) and output (journal digest) and compare against the caller/app's expected values; check exit_code is the one the application accepts (normally Halted(0)).
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: Skipping the image-ID comparison lets a receipt for a different guest program vouch for your journal; skipping the exit-code check lets a paused/split or errored execution (Halted(nonzero), Paused, SystemSplit) be presented as a completed successful run.

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: Digest (32B sha256-style in the Rust VerifiersConfig) encoding the root of the Merkle tree of control IDs for all sanctioned recursion circuits; on BN254 it is carried as a single field element (encoding from digest to field element is version-dependent and flagged as uncertain).
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: Pins the exact set of circuits (segment/lift/join/resolve) that may appear inside the proof chain.
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Verify the seal's control root equals the one the verifier's own parameters/verifying key were generated for (in Solidity it is a compile-time constant; in Rust the DefaultVerifier embeds it).
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: An attacker proves execution with their own modified circuit set whose control tree they computed themselves, producing a seal that internally verifies while asserting an arbitrary claim — total forgery with a real-looking receipt.

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: Digest identifying the bn254 stark-to-snark wrapper circuit; carried as a single BN254 field element among the public inputs.
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: Identifies which wrapper circuit the Groth16 verifying key corresponds to; ties the SNARK to a specific risc0 release's circuits.
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Must equal the constant associated with the hardcoded Groth16 verifying key; a mismatch means the seal was produced for a different circuit than the key being used.
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: If a deployer wires a verifying key from release A with control ids from release B (or accepts a caller-supplied control id), proofs from an unvetted circuit version verify; conversely honest receipts from the intended version are rejected or, worse, a matching attacker circuit/key pair is accepted.

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: Raw bytes, carried alongside the inner receipt, not inside the seal.
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: The guest's committed output; the seal never contains the journal itself, only its digest in claim.output.
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Compute sha256(journal_bytes) and require it equals claim.output; do this on every verify, not only at creation.
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: Journal substitution: any valid receipt can be repackaged with arbitrary journal bytes, so an attacker shows your image ID with a fabricated result.

components.pre: SystemState { pc: u32, merkle_root: Digest, digest: Digest } — machine state before the proven span; digest field is the image ID (sha256-style digest of the guest ELF), merkle_root is the root of the memory Merkle tree.
components.post: SystemState, same shape, at the end of the span; for a final receipt the merkle_root is the final memory commitment.
components.exit_code: ExitCode enum: SystemSplit | Halted(u8) | Paused; Halted(0) is the normal successful halt; Paused/SystemSplit relate to session continuation and are what 'verify' must distinguish from a finished run.
components.input: Digest — commitment to the guest input (added in 1.x; not present in 0.x claims).
components.output: Option<Digest> — Some(sha256(journal)) for a completed run; serialized as 8 digest words plus a 1-word present/none marker (exact marker encoding version-dependent).

claim_structure.digest_computation: The claim is serialized word-aligned via the Digestible/bytemuck path (52 words / 208 bytes in 1.x, including the Option marker) and hashed with sha256; Receipt::claim_digest() / ReceiptClaim::digest() return this value. The Groth16 public inputs carry this digest split into two ~128-bit limbs to fit the BN254 scalar field. Any change in claim fields or serialization across versions changes this digest, so digests are not comparable across risc0 versions.
claim_structure.uncertainty: Word-level offsets and the Option<Digest> marker value are reconstructed from the 1.x layout and the 592-byte ABI seal arithmetic (256+208+128=592); confirm against the specific release before relying on byte offsets.

binding_chain: 1. journal bytes -> sha256 -> journal digest; the VM records it as claim.output for a completed session.
2. ReceiptClaim assembled: pre.digest = image ID (program), pre/post.merkle_root = memory roots, exit_code, input digest, output = journal digest.
3. claim serialized (52 words) -> sha256 -> claim digest; this single 256-bit value is the canonical statement identifier.

4. Segment STARKs prove spans; the recursion pipeline (lift/join/resolve) produces a Succinct receipt whose proof internally checks that every consumed proof's control ID is a leaf of the control tree with root = control_root. This is where the control root enters: it is the whitelist of circuits, enforced in-circuit.

5. The Groth16 (bn254 control id) circuit verifies the succinct STARK and exposes public inputs: [claim digest limbs, control root, bn254 control id]. The bn254 control id ties the SNARK itself to the sanctioned wrapper circuit.

6. Seal = Groth16 proof (+ claim + public inputs in the ABI form). Verifier: recompute claim digest from claim bytes, match limbs, match control constants against verifying-key-bound values, pair-check, then bind to application data: claim.pre.digest == expected image ID, sha256(journal) == claim.output, exit_code acceptable.
Key invariant: the journal is bound only through claim.output inside the claim digest; nothing else in the seal touches the journal bytes.

circuit_version_dependent: Control root and all control IDs: derived from the recursion circuit set, they change with each risc0 release (0.x and 1.x are incompatible; 1.x point releases also changed them).
Groth16 verifying key, SEAL_SIZE, and the CONTROL_ROOT/BN254_CONTROL_ID constants hardcoded in the Ethereum verifier contract — all correspond to one release.
ReceiptClaim serialization layout (field set, Option marker) — changes shift the claim digest for identical semantics.
Segment/composite receipt shapes (0.x SegmentReceipt without claims vs 1.x claim-bearing segments).
2.x/3.x-era additions such as verifier-parameter/anchor mechanisms were introduced after my most confident knowledge; treat their specifics as unverified.
what_breaks_with_wrong_version: Benign failure: honest receipts from release A fail verification under release B's control root / verifying key — availability breaks, not safety.

Safety break: if a verifier is loosened to 'accept multiple control roots' or takes control constants from the receipt itself, an attacker proves with an attacker-built circuit set and forges arbitrary claims.
Digest confusion: claim digests computed under different serializations are incomparable; caching or comparing digests across versions misattributes results.
ABI confusion: parsing a seal with another release's offsets silently reads garbage as the claim, so recomputed digests and image-ID checks fail in confusing ways rather than cleanly.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Trusting a journal digest carried in the seal/API instead of hashing the journal bytes and comparing to claim.output on every verify.
common_verifier_bugs.catching_check: require(sha256(journal_bytes) == claim.output) inside the verify path, computed from the actual bytes presented.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Not validating exit code — accepting Paused, SystemSplit, or Halted(nonzero) as a completed successful commitment.
common_verifier_bugs.catching_check: require(claim.exit_code == Halted(0)) for final receipts; only continuations-oriented code may accept Paused/SystemSplit, and then it must resolve the continuation explicitly.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Accepting receipts with unresolved assumptions (composite receipts whose assumption receipts do not resolve, or continuation receipts presented as final).
common_verifier_bugs.catching_check: Reject any receipt whose claim still references unresolved assumptions; verify assumption resolution when consuming Composite receipts.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Recomputing the claim digest as sha256(imageId || journalDigest) or otherwise from a partial claim, instead of sha256 over the full serialized ReceiptClaim.
common_verifier_bugs.catching_check: Recompute the digest over the complete claim bytes as serialized by the matching risc0 version and compare against the public-input limbs.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Skipping BN254 canonicality checks on proof points (coordinates in range, on-curve, subgroup, non-infinity) before the pairing check.
common_verifier_bugs.catching_check: Explicit on-curve and field-range validation of pi_a/pi_b/pi_c, or use a verifier implementation known to enforce it, so malleated/degenerate proofs cannot verify.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Hardcoding or wiring control root / verifying key from a different risc0 release than the one that produced receipts (or 'supporting' several roots to make errors go away).
common_verifier_bugs.catching_check: Pin one release: assert the seal's control root and bn254 control id equal the constants bound to the deployed verifying key, and regenerate both together when upgrading the guest toolchain.

certainty_notes.receipt_kinds: High confidence that Composite/Succinct/Groth16 are the 1.x inner receipt variants and when each is produced; exact CompositeReceipt field names are medium confidence and likely shifted in 2.x.
certainty_notes.groth16_receipt_fields: Field names seal/claim/verifiers_config(control_root, bn254_control_id) are from the 1.x risc0-zkvm design with medium-high confidence; the 592-byte ABI seal total is well-attested, but the internal byte ordering (proof/claim/limbs) is reconstructed from size arithmetic (256+208+128) and is medium-low confidence — verify offsets against the risc0-ethereum release you target.
certainty_notes.claim_structure: High confidence on the field set (pre/post SystemState with pc, merkle_root, digest=image ID; exit_code variants; input; output Option) and sha256-based Digestible digest; medium confidence on the 52-word size and the Option<Digest> marker encoding.
certainty_notes.binding_chain: High confidence on the chain's shape (journal->output digest, claim digest as public input, control root as circuit whitelist enforced in-circuit, VK pinning the wrapper); medium confidence on the exact limb split of the claim digest and the digest-to-BN254-field-element encoding.
certainty_notes.version_coupling: High confidence that control root/control IDs/VK/claim serialization are release-coupled and that mismatched versions fail benignly while loosened checks enable forgery; low confidence on specific 2.x/3.x verifier-parameter mechanisms.
certainty_notes.common_verifier_bugs: Journal-check omission, exit-code omission, control-root pinning, and non-canonical point issues are known classes in risc0-adjacent verification; the unresolved-assumptions and partial-claim-digest bugs are plausible constructions labeled as such rather than documented incidents.

data.annex_basis: Directive 2008/48/EC Annex I Part I (basic equation) / Directive (EU) 2023/2225 Annex III equivalent; no numbered numerical example recalled
computation: Solve Σ C_k / (1+X)^{t_k} = Σ D_l / (1+X)^{s_l} for X

receipt_kinds.when_produced: Direct output of multi-segment execution; vector of SegmentReceipts (one STARK per segment via RISC-V circuit) plus optional assumption receipts; used when full segment details or assumptions are retained
After recursion (lift + join/resolve) aggregates a CompositeReceipt (or prior SuccinctReceipts) into a single STARK via the recursion circuit; constant-size independent of segment count
After STARK-to-SNARK compression: a SuccinctReceipt is verified inside the Groth16 circuit (identity_p254 + compress) producing a BN254 Groth16 proof; intended for on-chain / succinct verification
Dev-mode only; no cryptographic seal; for rapid prototyping

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: Vec<u8> (or structured a/b/c points after selector); typically 4-byte selector + Groth16 proof (A, B, C on BN254)
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: The opaque Groth16 proof attesting that the recursion/identity circuit accepted the claim under the control root
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Parse selector, decode proof points, run pairing check against fixed verifying key with public inputs (split control_root, split claim_digest, bn254_control_id)
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: Arbitrary forged seal accepted; any claim/journal can be asserted without a valid proof

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: MaybePruned<ReceiptClaim> (full struct or Digest)
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: The public statement being proven: pre/post system state, exit code, input digest, output (journal + assumptions)
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Recompute claim.digest() and ensure it matches the claim digest fed as public input to the Groth16 verifier; for ok() receipts also check exit_code == Halted(0) and journal matches
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: Journal/claim substitution: attacker supplies a valid seal for one claim but a different journal or image_id

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: Digest (hash of Groth16ReceiptVerifierParameters)
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: Fingerprint of the expected control_root, bn254_control_id and verifying_key; allows version detection without embedding full parameters
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Compare against the digest of the trusted parameters the verifier was compiled/configured with; reject mismatch
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: Cross-version confusion: a seal produced under an old/new control root or VK is accepted by a verifier expecting different parameters

components.pre: MaybePruned<SystemState> or Digest (image_id / pre-state merkle root + pc; for ok receipts often just the image_id)
components.post: MaybePruned<SystemState> (post-state pc + memory merkle root; often zeroed for Halted(0))
components.input: Digest (commitment to guest input; frequently zero)
components.output: MaybePruned<Output> where Output = { journal: Digest (SHA-256 of journal bytes), assumptions: Digest }

claim_structure.claim_digest_computation: Tagged structural hash (sha256 of tag 'risc0.ReceiptClaim' || input || pre || post.digest() || output.digest() || exit_code packing || length); exact byte layout is version-stable within a major release but uses the risc0 tagged-struct encoding. For the common 'ok' case: ReceiptClaim::ok(image_id, journal_digest) produces a claim whose digest is the value placed in Groth16 public inputs.

binding_chain: journal bytes → SHA-256 → journal_digest (inside Output)
Output + pre/post/exit/input → tagged ReceiptClaim → claim_digest
claim_digest is split into two 128-bit limbs (byte-reversed) and supplied as public inputs to the Groth16 circuit together with the two limbs of control_root and the bn254_control_id
Groth16 seal is a proof that the recursion/identity circuit accepted exactly those public inputs under the verifying key

control_root (Merkle root of allowed recursion control IDs) and verifying_key are fixed parameters of the verifier; they bind the seal to a specific circuit version; bn254_control_id identifies the Poseidon-BN254 control program used in the final recursion step

circuit_version_dependent: control_root (and the set of control IDs it commits to)
selector (first 4 bytes of seal, derived from parameters)
exact tagged-hash encoding of ReceiptClaim / SystemState / Output (minor layout changes across major releases)
version_coupling.what_breaks_wrong_version: Pairing check fails (wrong VK), or selector mismatch aborts early, or claim_digest computed with different tagging does not match the public input the seal was generated for; a verifier that ignores the parameters digest can accept a seal from an incompatible recursion circuit that proves a different statement

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Accepting seal without checking claim_digest == public-input claim limbs
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches_it: Recompute claim.digest() from the supplied ReceiptClaim / journal and compare to the value reconstructed from the Groth16 public signals

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Ignoring exit_code / treating any Halted(n) as success
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches_it: Explicitly require ExitCode::Halted(0) (or the application-specific success code) after claim decoding

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Not verifying journal bytes hash to the journal_digest inside the claim
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches_it: SHA-256(journal.bytes) == claim.output.journal

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Using a hard-coded or wrong control_root / VK for the seal's selector
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches_it: Selector match + parameters-digest equality against the trusted Groth16ReceiptVerifierParameters

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Treating MaybePruned::Pruned values as trusted without the seal binding them
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches_it: Only accept pruned fields when the claim_digest (which includes those digests) has been verified by the seal

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Forgetting to reject non-empty assumptions on an unconditional receipt
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches_it: Assert assumptions digest is zero (or explicitly resolve every assumption) when the receipt is presented as unconditional

data.formula_basis: ES_alpha = sigma * phi(z_{1-alpha}) / (1-alpha) for P&L ~ N(mu,sigma^2); VaR_alpha = mu + sigma * z_{1-alpha} where Phi(z_{1-alpha}) = 1-alpha; MAR33 anchor: parametric normal ES is the theoretical benchmark for the 97.5% ES standard.
data.weakest_point: Implementation defect: conflating ES multiplier (2.3376) with VaR multiplier (1.9600) understates tail-risk capital by 16.2% (ratio VaR/ES = 0.8385).

data.formula_basis: ES_alpha = sigma * phi(z_{1-alpha}) / (1-alpha) for P&L ~ N(mu,sigma^2); VaR_alpha = mu + sigma * z_{1-alpha} where Phi(z_{1-alpha}) = 1-alpha; MAR33 anchor: the 99% ES is used for stress testing and model validation comparisons.
data.weakest_point: Implementation defect: conflating ES multiplier (2.6650) with VaR multiplier (2.3263) understates tail-risk capital by 12.7% (ratio VaR/ES = 0.8729).

data.formula_basis: ES_LH = ES_10d * sqrt(LH / 10); MAR33 section 33.3: ES scaled by square root of liquidity horizon over 10-day base horizon for modellable risk factors.
data.weakest_point: The sqrt(LH/10) rule assumes i.i.d. returns with constant volatility; autocorrelation or volatility clustering in credit spreads invalidates the scaling.

computation.step_5_fractional_treatment_convention: Acerbi-Tasche fractional order statistic: ES = [sum_{i=1}^{floor(k)} L_(i) + (k - floor(k)) * L_(ceil(k))] / k

data.formula_basis: ES_alpha = (1/k) * [sum_{i=1}^{floor(k)} L_(i) + (k - floor(k)) * L_(ceil(k))] where k = n(1-alpha) and L_(i) are ascending-sorted P&L; MAR33 section 33.2: ES is the average of P&L in the tail beyond the VaR quantile.
data.weakest_point: With n=20 and alpha=97.5%, the tail contains k=0.5 observations, so ES equals the single worst observation (-8.5) under standard interpolation conventions; the estimate has zero statistical robustness and is entirely sample-dependent.

data.rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.2.3 — ES6 Number.prototype.toString() defines -0 as "0"
data.divergence_trap: Some C#/Java or custom serializers output "-0" instead of "0"

data.vector_name: 1e21 boundary — exponent notation threshold for large integers
data.rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.2.3 — ES6 toString uses plain digits below 1e21, exponent form at and above 1e21
data.divergence_trap: Python json.dumps outputs "1e+20" (scientific notation) for 1e20 instead of the full integer string; also fails to sort keys

data.vector_name: 1e-7 boundary — exponent notation threshold for small decimals
data.rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.2.3 — ES6 toString uses plain decimals down to 1e-6, exponent form at and below 1e-7

data.vector_name: 2^53 + 1 is not exactly representable — rounds to 2^53

data.divergence_trap: Python json.dumps (and other arbitrary-precision-integer parsers) preserve the exact literal "9007199254740993" instead of the rounded double value

data.rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.2.2 — solidus is not in the mandatory escape set (only quotation mark, reverse solidus, and U+0000-U+001F)

data.vector_name: UTF-16 code-unit ordering — non-BMP character sorts before U+E000
data.rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.2.1 — keys sorted by UTF-16 code unit value; U+10000 is surrogate pair [0xD800,0xDC00] and 0xD800 (55296) < 0xE000 (57344)
data.divergence_trap: Python sort_keys (and any code-point-based sorter) orders U+E000 (57344) before U+10000 (65536), producing {"":2,"𐀀":1}

data.vector_name: Unicode normalization is NOT performed — distinct keys remain distinct
data.rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.2.2 — strings serialized as-is without Unicode normalization; §3.2.2.1 keys sorted by UTF-16 code unit
data.divergence_trap: NFC-normalizing serializers (e.g., some Go or ICU-based implementations) would normalize U+0041 U+030A to U+00C5, causing either a duplicate-key error or a single merged key

data.vector_name: Control character U+001F escaped as lowercase \u001f
data.rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.2.2 — control characters U+0000-U+001F MUST be escaped as \uXXXX with lowercase hex digits
data.divergence_trap: Some serializers use uppercase \u001F, or use non-standard short escapes like \x1f, or fail to escape control characters above U+0019

data.vector_name: Empty object and empty array preserved with recursive key sorting
data.rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.2.1 — objects sorted by key; arrays and empty structures preserved as-is
data.divergence_trap: None for this trivial case, but naive implementations that strip whitespace or reorder structural tokens produce divergent compact forms

data.vector_name: Array element order MUST NOT be changed
data.rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.2.1 — array element order is preserved; only object property names are sorted
data.divergence_trap: A naive "sort everything recursively" implementation (e.g., a generic tree canonicalizer) sorts array elements to [1,2,3]

data.vector_name: Integer beyond 2^53 loses precision in double serialization
data.divergence_trap: Python json.dumps (arbitrary-precision integers) and other exact-integer parsers output the full unrounded literal "12345678901234567890"

data.rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.2.3 — ES6 toString(0) is "0"; subnormal values below double minimum underflow to 0
