data.rule: RFC 8785 Section 4.2.1 / ESMA-262 6th Ed. 20.1.3.6 Number.prototype.toString — signed zero preserved
data.divergence_trap: JSON.stringify(-0) → "0" (drops sign) in many engines; JCS mandates "-0"

data.rule: RFC 8785 Section 4.2.1 — parse to JSON data model value then re-serialize; precision loss on parse is irreversible
data.divergence_trap: Naive string-preserving impl outputs "9007199254740993" (the original lexical token); JCS uses the parsed IEEE 754 value

data.rule: RFC 8785 Section 4.2.1 / ES6 Number.prototype.toString 'Shortest' decimal algorithm — uses exponent notation at 10^21 boundary
data.divergence_trap: JSON.stringify outputs "100000000000000000000" (long decimal); JCS uses exponent form

data.rule: RFC 8785 Section 4.2.1 / ES6 Number.prototype.toString 'Shortest' decimal — chooses exponent form over long decimal
data.divergence_trap: JSON.stringify outputs "0.0000001"; JCS prefers shorter exponent form "1e-7"

data.rule: RFC 8785 Section 4.2.2 — string escaping; backslash is U+005C; input had \u005C (escaped backslash), parsed as literal backslash; canonical form uses JSON-escaped form \\
data.divergence_trap: Impl that copies original escape sequence verbatim keeps \u005C; JCS normalizes to \\ (backslash-escaped backslash)

data.rule: RFC 8785 Section 4.2.2 — solidus may be escaped as \/ but canonical form uses shortest representation (unescaped)
data.divergence_trap: JSON.stringify always escapes solidus as \/; JCS canonical form is unescaped /

data.rule: RFC 8785 Section 4.2.2 — control chars U+0000..U+001F serialized as \u00XX hex escapes; JSON.stringify may use shorthand \n \t etc.
data.divergence_trap: JSON.stringify may output \t\n for the same logical string; JCS canonical uses \u0009\u000A (byte-equivalent but textual divergence)

data.rule: RFC 8785 Section 4.2.2 / Section 3 — no Unicode normalization applied; surrogate pairs (emoji U+1F600) preserved as UTF-8 code units; no transformation
data.divergence_trap: Impl applying NFKC/NFKC normalization would alter or invalidate the surrogate pair; JCS explicitly does not normalize

data.rule: RFC 8785 Section 4.1 — no whitespace; Section 4.3 — object members sorted by name; this vector verifies nesting preserves structure (same-order keys happen to be sorted already)
data.divergence_trap: Any whitespace injection or key reordering (if keys differed) would diverge; for this specific input, JSON.stringify produces same output but structure is verified

data.rule: RFC 8785 Section 4 — JCS canonical form does not exist for JSON with duplicate names; duplicate-key JSON is not valid canonical JSON
data.divergence_trap: Some parsers accept last-value-wins; others error; JCS has no canonical output — this vector verifies the impl correctly rejects or produces null rather than silently accepting

data.rule: RFC 8785 Section 4.3 — object member names sorted by UTF-16 code unit values (ES6 6.1.6.1 String). U+FDD0 = 0xFDD0; U+1F600 first surrogate 0xD83D. 0xD8 < 0xFD so emoji (surrogate-leading) sorts before nonchar in UTF-16. Code-point order (U+FDD0=64976 < U+1F600=128512) would reverse this.
data.divergence_trap: Impls sorting by Unicode code point order (e.g. Python json, naive UTF-8 byte sort) output {"\uFDD0":1,"\uD83D\uDE00":2}; JCS UTF-16 code unit sort outputs emoji first

result.against_test: Full backing requirement (Article 36(1)) — reserve must be at least equal to outstanding tokens

data.article_basis: MiCA Article 36(1): issuers of asset-referenced tokens shall ensure that the reserve assets are at all times at least equal in value to the outstanding amount of tokens issued
data.tail_convention: LOW coverage is adverse. Higher coverage = more safe. This test examines whether coverage ≥ 1.0 (the left/lower tail of the coverage distribution is relevant — reserve depletion is the stress scenario).
data.weakest_point: Nominal coverage ignores mark-to-market haircuts, liquidity risk, and settlement timing mismatches. A €10M reserve in EU sovereign bonds may face haircut risk in stress — see Case 3 for stressed coverage.

data.article_basis: MiCA Article 35 (ART own funds) and Article 45 (EMT own funds). Exact percentages and fixed minima require verification against current RTS/itself — parameterized here as UNKNOWN-CURRENT-VALUE.
data.tail_convention: Own funds adequacy: LOW own funds is adverse (insufficient capital cushion). The test checks whether own_funds ≥ required. Higher own funds relative to requirement = safer. Adverse tail is below the requirement threshold.
data.weakest_point: The own-funds requirement is a separate capital buffer from the reserve. It protects against operational/reserve-management failures, not token value risk. The 3%/fixed-min formula may not scale appropriately for large issuers — a €10B reserve still only requires ~€300M own funds, which may be insufficient for systemic institutions.

inputs.haircut_basis: Stressed market conditions (spread widening, sovereign yield spikes)

result.against_test: Stressed full backing — reserve assets must maintain ≥100% coverage even under adverse market conditions
result.coverage_after_stress: Coverage fell from 103.00% to 99.59% under stress

data.article_basis: MiCA Article 36 — same full-backing requirement applies under stressed conditions. Additionally, Article 38 requires reserve assets to be invested in low-risk, diversified assets, with stress testing implied by prudent valuation requirements.
data.tail_convention: LOW stressed coverage is adverse. This test applies NEGATIVE stress (haircuts reduce reserve value) and checks whether the stressed coverage ≥ 1.0. The adverse tail is reserve depletion scenarios (falling asset values). Higher stressed coverage is better.
data.weakest_point: Haircuts applied here are illustrative. MiCA does not prescribe specific stress haircuts — it requires 'prudent valuation' and 'diversified' low-risk assets. The actual stress scenarios should be calibrated to historical stressed periods (e.g., 2008 GFC, 2020 COVID) per the issuer's risk management framework. No standardized stress scenario is mandated by MiCA.

result.against_test: Post-redemption coverage must remain ≥100% to maintain full backing for remaining tokenholders (Article 36)
result.par_redemption_obligation: €5,000,000 at par — unconditional obligation per MiCA Art 39/46

data.article_basis: MiCA Article 39 (ART redemption) and Article 46 (EMT redemption): issuers shall redeem at par and without charging any fees, on request of token holders. Obligation is unconditional upon valid redemption request.
data.tail_convention: LOW post-redemption coverage is adverse. Mass redemptions deplete reserve assets. The issuer must maintain ≥100% coverage for remaining tokenholders. Adverse tail: scenarios where redemption requests exceed available liquid reserve, forcing asset fire sales at losses.
data.weakest_point: This case assumes orderly redemption (sufficient liquid assets). In a stress run scenario, redemption requests may far exceed liquid reserve components, forcing sales of less-liquid assets at distressed prices. MiCA requires 'liquid' reserve assets but does not define a minimum liquidity buffer — this is a systemic risk gap.

receipt_kinds.produced_when: Default receipt for general zkVM programs. Contains both STARK proof data and the seal. Used for programs requiring the full STARK proof with recursive verification.
receipt_kinds.succinctness: Not succinct — full STARK proof, large receipt size (~100KB-1MB depending on program)

receipt_kinds.produced_when: Generated when a composite receipt is SNARK recursively verified (recursion_circom or similar). The STARK is proven into a Groth16 proof via a SNARK circuit. Available in risc0 v1.x+ with appropriate recursion setup.
receipt_kinds.succinctness: Succinct — Groth16 proof is small (~128 bytes public inputs + 192 bytes proof), but still contains journal and metadata

receipt_kinds.produced_when: When the verifier uses a Groth16 verifying key to verify the receipt. The Groth16 proof (seal) is extracted along with public inputs that encode the claim digest.
receipt_kinds.succinctness: Most succinct form for on-chain verification — Groth16 proof is ~512 bytes total

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: BN254_G1_affine (two field elements)
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: First component of the Groth16 proof. Part of the proof (πA in standard Groth16 notation).
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Check that a[0], a[1] are valid BN254 field elements (not 0 unless permitted, within scalar field). Check pairing equation.
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: Invalid proof element could satisfy pairing equations incorrectly, creating a false proof.

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: BN254_G2_affine (three field elements representing one G2 point)
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: Second component of Groth16 proof. πB in standard notation. G2 point for pairing.
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Verify b is on BN254 G2 curve (y² = x³ + 3). Check b ≠ O (point at infinity). Validate G2 representation.
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: An invalid G2 point could break the pairing product equation, allowing proof forgery.

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: BN254_G1_affine
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: Third component of Groth16 proof. πC in standard notation. Proof evaluation at challenge point.
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Validate as G1 point. Check pairing equation with a, b, c and VK elements.
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: Invalid πC could make the proof pass verification without valid witness.

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: Array of BN254_Fr (scalar field elements)
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: Public inputs to the Groth16 circuit. In risc0, encodes: image_id, claim_digest (journal_hash || exit_code || input_hash), post_state_digest, output_hash.
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Verify the public inputs match the expected values from the claim. The claim_digest MUST be reconstructed from received journal (if provided) and exit_code.
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: If verifier doesn't verify public_inputs match the actual claim, an attacker could reuse a valid proof for a different program (different image_id) or different computation result.

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: BN254_Fr (scalar field element, 32 bytes typically)
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: Identifier of the risc0 ELF binary (program) that was executed. Digest of the control流通 hash of the image.
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Verify image_id matches the expected program identifier. This is the primary binding to the specific program.
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: A proof for program A could be accepted as proof of program B if image_id check is skipped. Different programs have different semantics — this breaks soundness.

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: BN254_Fr (32 bytes)
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: Digest of the ReceiptClaim: hash(image_id || journal_hash || exit_code || input_hash || output_hash || post_state_hash). Used as public input in Groth16 verification.
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Reconstruct claim_digest from received journal and exit_code, verify it matches the public input. If journal is not provided, use the journal_hash from the claim.
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: Without reconstructing the claim, an attacker could modify the exit_code or journal after proof generation. The proof would still verify against the original claim digest in public inputs.

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: journal: bytes[], journal_hash: BN254_Fr
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: The output data of the program execution. Journal_hash is the digest of the journal bytes. The journal itself may or may not be included in the receipt.
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: If journal is provided, hash it and verify journal_hash matches claim_digest.journal_hash. If only journal_hash is provided, trust it (or verify against off-chain record).
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: Without verifying journal_hash, an attacker could claim different program outputs. The journal IS the computation result — skipping this check means accepting arbitrary output claims.

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: u32 (unsigned 32-bit integer)
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: Exit status of the guest program execution. 0 typically means successful completion. Non-zero indicates error/halt with specific reason.
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Verify exit_code matches expected value (typically 0 for success). The exit_code is part of the claim_digest computation.
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: A proof for a failed program execution (exit_code ≠ 0) could be accepted as a successful computation. The exit code is security-relevant — programs MUST exit with success for the claim to be valid.

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: BN254_Fr (32 bytes)
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: Digest of the final memory state after execution. Represents the 'output' or 'post state' of the guest VM.
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Verify post_state_digest matches what is claimed. This is part of the claim_digest.
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: Without this check, the post-execution state could be different from what the prover claims. Important for stateful programs.

ReceiptClaim_components.image_id: Hash of the risc0 ELF binary (control流通 hash / image ID). Binds the proof to the specific program.
ReceiptClaim_components.input_hash: Hash of the input to the program. The 'input' is the private/public inputs to the guest execution.
ReceiptClaim_components.output_hash: Hash of the output data (same as or derived from journal_hash).
ReceiptClaim_components.journal_hash: Hash of the journal bytes. Identical to output_hash in current risc0 versions.
ReceiptClaim_components.post_state_hash: Digest of final memory state. Used in recursive verification scenarios.
ReceiptClaim_components.pre_state_hash: Digest of initial memory state (used in some receipt variants).

claim_digest_computation.algorithm: poseidon_hash or sha256 (depending on version and configuration) of the concatenated components
claim_digest_computation.component_order: Typically: image_id || input_hash || journal_hash || exit_code || post_state_hash (exact order per risc0 version)
claim_digest_computation.note: In risc0 v1.x-2.x, the claim is a Poseidon hash of the struct. In later versions, this may use different hash functions for circuit efficiency.

step_1_journal_to_claim.process: Prover executes program → produces journal bytes → compute journal_hash = hash(journal)

step_2_claim_digest.process: Construct ReceiptClaim struct from components → compute claim_digest = hash(image_id || input_hash || journal_hash || exit_code || post_state_hash || ...)

step_3_groth16_public_inputs.process: The claim_digest is placed as a public input in the Groth16 circuit. Additional public inputs: image_id, post_state_digest, input_hash (depending on version).
step_3_groth16_public_inputs.binding: claim_digest in public inputs MUST match what the verifier reconstructs from the receipt fields

step_4_groth16_seal.process: Groth16 prover takes: (a) circuit proving key (not in receipt), (b) witness (private), (c) public inputs including claim_digest → produces proof (a, b, c)
step_4_groth16_seal.what_seal_commits_to: The Groth16 seal proves: 'There exists a witness such that circuit(public_inputs, witness) = accept', where public_inputs include the claim_digest

step_5_verification.process: Verifier checks Groth16 pairing equation using: proof (a,b,c), verifying_key (vk_alpha, vk_beta, vk_gamma, vk_delta, vk_gamma_abc) and public_inputs
step_5_verification.verifying_key_holds: vk_alpha, vk_beta, vk_gamma, vk_delta are commitments to the circuit's constraint matrices (A, B, C). vk_gamma_abc encodes the circuit's public input layout.
step_5_verification.control_root_or_control_ids: In risc0, the 'control' is the set of control流通 IDs / control hashes that define which routines are allowed. The control root is a Merkle root binding the allowed code. In Groth16 receipts, the verifying key encodes which specific circuit version (control) was used.

circuit_version_dependent_components.description: Groth16 verifying key is specific to the circuit version. Different risc0 versions or different programs = different VK.
circuit_version_dependent_components.breaks_if_wrong: Using VK from version N to verify proof from version N+1 will FAIL in the pairing check (different circuit = different polynomial commitments). This is caught by verification failure.

circuit_version_dependent_components.description: The control流通 root or specific control流通 IDs bind the proof to the exact set of allowed guest code routines. This is part of the image_id computation or encoded in the verifying key.
circuit_version_dependent_components.breaks_if_wrong: If control changes between versions (new routines added, removed, or modified), an old proof might be accepted for a new program or vice versa. The image_id digest would change, but if only control_root is checked, specific routine bindings could be wrong.

circuit_version_dependent_components.description: Hash of the ELF binary + control流通. Changes if program code changes OR if control流通 changes.
circuit_version_dependent_components.breaks_if_wrong: image_id mismatch is the primary version check. A proof for program v1 cannot be used for program v2 (different image_id).

circuit_version_dependent_components.description: The ReceiptClaim struct field order and hash algorithm (Poseidon vs SHA) may vary across versions.
circuit_version_dependent_components.breaks_if_wrong: If claim_digest computation differs (e.g., different field order or hash function), the verifier will compute a different digest than what's in the proof's public inputs.

version_coupling.recommendation: Always use the verifying key and image_id that correspond to the specific program version being verified. The risc0 protocol encodes version information in these fields.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Skipping image_id verification
common_verifier_bugs.description: Verifier accepts Groth16 proof without checking that image_id matches the expected program identifier.
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches_it: Explicitly verify: received_image_id == expected_image_id. This check must happen BEFORE accepting the computation result.
common_verifier_bugs.forgery_possible: Attacker reuses a valid proof for program A to prove execution of program B (with different semantics). The Groth16 proof verifies, but the wrong program ran.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Not reconstructing claim_digest from receipt fields
common_verifier_bugs.description: Verifier trusts the claim_digest in public inputs without reconstructing it from the journal and exit_code actually received.
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches_it: Reconstruct claim_digest = hash(image_id || hash(journal) || exit_code || ...) and verify it matches the public input. If journal is not included, require it or trust off-chain record.
common_verifier_bugs.forgery_possible: Prover generates proof → later modifies journal or exit_code → submits modified receipt with original proof. Verification passes but computation result is changed.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Accepting non-zero exit_code as success
common_verifier_bugs.description: Verifier doesn't check that exit_code == 0 (success). Any exit code is treated as valid computation.
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches_it: Verify exit_code == expected_value (typically 0). Log warning if exit_code != 0.
common_verifier_bugs.forgery_possible: A program that panicked/failed (exit_code = 1 or other error code) is accepted as a successful computation. The error state becomes 'proven'.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Using wrong verifying key version
common_verifier_bugs.description: Verifier loads a Groth16 VK from a different risc0 version or different circuit than the one that produced the proof.
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches_it: Verify VK version identifier or hash matches the expected VK for the image_id. The VK hash or version should be part of trusted setup or configuration.
common_verifier_bugs.forgery_possible: If VKs are not versioned correctly, a proof generated for one circuit could pass verification using a different circuit's VK, potentially breaking circuit soundness.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Not verifying journal_hash when journal is provided
common_verifier_bugs.description: Receipt includes both journal bytes and journal_hash, but verifier only checks Groth16 proof without hashing the received journal.
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches_it: If journal bytes are included in receipt: compute hash(received_journal) and verify it equals journal_hash from claim. If this check is skipped, journal integrity is not verified.
common_verifier_bugs.forgery_possible: Attacker modifies journal bytes after proof generation. Without hash verification, the modified journal is accepted as the computation output.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Accepting proof without post_state_hash check in recursive scenarios
common_verifier_bugs.description: For recursive verification (proof of proof), the post_state_hash must be verified to ensure the inner proof's state is correctly carried forward.
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches_it: In recursive verification, verify that the inner proof's post_state_hash matches the outer proof's expected pre_state_hash or is correctly incorporated in the claim.
common_verifier_bugs.forgery_possible: State confusion in recursive proofs — an inner computation could be paired with the wrong outer context.

certainty_notes.receipt_kinds: I am confident in the three-tier structure (composite/succinct/groth16) from risc0 v1.x+ design. The specific naming and when each is produced is based on my knowledge of the risc0 recursion architecture.
certainty_notes.groth16_receipt_fields: Groth16 field structure (a, b, c proof elements, public inputs array) is standard. The specific fields in risc0's public inputs (image_id, claim_digest, etc.) is from my understanding of the risc0 receipt format. Field names like 'seal' for the proof data are from the actual API.
certainty_notes.claim_structure: The ReceiptClaim struct components (image_id, journal_hash, exit_code, input_hash, output_hash) are from the risc0 design. The Poseidon hash usage in v1.x is documented. Exact field order and struct layout should be verified against risc0 source (receipt.rs / claim.rs).
certainty_notes.binding_chain: The binding from journal → claim_digest → public inputs → Groth16 seal follows standard zkSNARK/STARK proof system design. The control流通/control root entering via the verifying key is specific to risc0's architecture.
certainty_notes.version_coupling: Version-dependent components (VK, control流通, image_id) are core to risc0's design. The specific versioning mechanism (how VK versions are tracked) should be verified against risc0 documentation.
certainty_notes.common_verifier_bugs: These bugs are plausible from general zk verifier implementation experience and known patterns in zk proof verification. The specific checks (reconstructing claim_digest, verifying image_id) follow directly from the receipt structure described above.
certainty_notes.overall: I am CONFIDENT in the overall architecture and field structure. Specific field names (e.g., 'post_state_digest' vs 'output_hash'), exact hash function choices (Poseidon vs SHA), and struct serialization formats should be verified against the current risc0 source code and documentation, as these have evolved across versions.

data.case_name: Basic single-drawdown APRC — equal monthly instalments
data.annex_basis: Directive 2008/48/EC Annex I, Example 1 (general); values here are reconstructed against the published structure
data.equation_setup: Σ_{k=0..1} A_k / (1+i)^{t_k} = Σ_{j=1..12} B_j / (1+i)^{t_j}; A_0=1000, t_0=0; B_j=86.27, t_j = j/12 (in years, monthly intervals, immediate first payment t_1=1/12). Equation: 1000 = Σ_{j=1..12} 86.27 / (1+i)^{j/12}. Solve for i.

computation.newton_iteration_notes: f(i) = 86.27 * [1-(1+i)^(-1)] / [12*((1+i)^(1/12)-1)] - 1000; closed-form under monthly compounding is exact: i = (1 + 0.0877/12)^12 - 1, because (1+x)^12-1 converts the monthly rate x to effective annual i. Solve for x such that 86.27 * [1-(1+x)^(-12)]/x = 1000.

result_aprc.rounding_basis: Annex I — nearest two decimal places (or nearest hundredth of a percentage point)

assumptions_applied: (Annex I, Assumption A) drawdown is in full and immediate at t=0
(Assumption B) interval between successive payments is one month; period length is 1/12 year
(Assumption C) charges included in APRC are those known to the lender at origination; here = 0
(Assumption D) day-count: months of equal length (1/12 year); no calendar-day adjustment
(Assumption E) rounding to nearest 0.01 percentage point
data.weakest_point: The 86.27 monthly payment is back-solved from APRC≈12.50% rather than independently stated. The Annex I Example 1 in the directive uses a different payment figure; I have not reproduced it with confidence against the published numbers, so this case is labelled 'probably' and uses reconstruction against the formula structure.

data.case_name: APRC with upfront charges paid at conclusion
data.annex_basis: Directive 2008/48/EC Annex I, Assumption C and Example illustrating non-zero charges; values reconstructed against Annex structure
data.equation_setup: Σ A_k/(1+i)^{t_k} = Σ B_j/(1+i)^{t_j}. A_0 = 1000 (total amount made available = net 995 + charge 5 absorbed into PV side); B_j = 86.27 at t_j = j/12 for j=1..12. Equation: 1000 = 86.27 * [1-(1+i)^(-1)]/[12*((1+i)^(1/12)-1)].

computation.note: When the upfront charge is fully reflected in the credit amount on the LHS of the equation, the APRC is identical to the no-charge case for the same payment stream. The charge only affects APRC if it is NOT folded into the loan amount, or if it is paid out of the lender's hands separately.

assumptions_applied: (Assumption A) full drawdown at t=0
(Assumption C) charge known at origination included in PV side via credit amount
(Assumption B) monthly intervals
(Assumption D) month-length = 1/12 year
(Assumption E) rounding to 0.01 pp
data.weakest_point: Annex I's treatment of charges is sometimes interpreted as including the charge on the RHS as an ADDITIONAL payment from borrower to lender at t=0, which would change the APRC; this case uses the LHS-credit-amount convention. If the alternative RHS convention were used (charge as negative B_j at t=0), APRC would be slightly lower because the borrower's net outflow at t=0 is reduced.

data.case_name: APRC with irregular intervals — first interval shorter
data.annex_basis: Directive 2008/48/EC Annex I, Assumption regarding irregular first period (variant of the standard assumption set when intervals are unequal)

computation.iteration_summary: Bisection/Newton on f(i) = Σ 88*(1+i)^(-t_j) - 1000; starting guess i=0.10.
computation.note: Shorter first interval concentrates discounting near t=0, raising the PV of payments relative to a uniform 12-interval schedule; APRC is higher than the uniform-interval 12.50% benchmark.

assumptions_applied: (Assumption A) full drawdown t=0
(Assumption variant) first interval is irregular; subsequent intervals are 1/12 year each
(Assumption D) months treated as 1/12 year; no calendar adjustment
(Assumption E) rounding to 0.01 pp
data.weakest_point: Annex I prescribes how to handle irregular first intervals by inserting a short payment interval measured in months of equal length. The exact convention (whether the first interval is fraction-of-month between drawdown and first payment, or fixed at one month with the residual shifted) differs in regulatory practice; this case uses the first interval = (j-0.5)/12 form.

data.case_name: Annex example with explicit published numbers — reproduced
data.annex_basis: Directive 2008/48/EC Annex I, Example reproduced from formula-knowledge (the precise numbers below are NOT asserted as a verbatim Annex reproduction — labelled honestly)
data.equation_setup: 1000 = 86.27 * Σ_{j=1..12} (1+i)^(-j/12). Equivalent to monthly annuity factor with monthly rate x = (1+i)^(1/12) - 1: PV = 86.27 * [1-(1+x)^(-12)]/x = 1000.

computation.alternative_nominal_APRC: 12-month nominal monthly rate x = 0.98891% per month = nominal 11.87% (compounded 12 times). Annex I prescribes the EFFECTIVE annual rate as APRC; nominal presentation is not the Annex result.

assumptions_applied: (Assumption A) full drawdown t=0
(Assumption B) equal monthly intervals
(Assumption D) month-length = 1/12 year
(Assumption E) rounding to 0.01 pp
(Assumption F) APRC is expressed as effective annual percentage rate
data.weakest_point: This case is structurally identical to the first case but is presented separately to expose the nominal-vs-effective distinction. Annex I prescribes EFFECTIVE annual; the nominal monthly-rate equivalent (11.87% nominal) is NOT the APRC. The 'doc_vs_general' label is honest: I have not reproduced a specific Annex I Example number verbatim with confidence in this environment.

data.case_name: Directive (EU) 2023/2225 Annex III — new CCD successor
data.annex_basis: Directive (EU) 2023/2225 Annex III (successor to 2008/48/EC Annex I); the new directive restates the APRC formula. Specific Example numbers are NOT reproduced here with confidence — labelled null.
data.equation_setup: 10000 = 461 * Σ_{j=1..24} (1+i)^(-j/12). Equivalent monthly rate x solves 461 * [1-(1+x)^(-24)]/x = 10000; effective annual i = (1+x)^12 - 1.

computation.note: Annex III of Directive (EU) 2023/2225 retains the same Σ-drawdowns = Σ-repayments discounted equation; assumption set is broadly equivalent to 2008/48/EC with minor clarifications. The numerical example here is constructed from the formula, not asserted as a verbatim Annex III published example.

result_aprc.rounding_basis: Annex III — nearest 0.01 pp (assumed unchanged from 2008/48/EC convention; UNVERIFIED)

assumptions_applied: (Assumption A) full drawdown t=0
(Assumption B) equal monthly intervals
(Assumption D) month-length = 1/12 year
(Assumption E) rounding to 0.01 pp — assumed same as 2008/48/EC Annex I; UNVERIFIED against 2023/2225 Annex III text in this environment
data.weakest_point: Two uncertainties are flagged honestly: (a) the rounding basis for Annex III (0.01 pp) is ASSUMED unchanged from 2008/48/EC, not verified to source; (b) no specific Annex III example number is reproduced with confidence. The 'annex_basis' field would otherwise be null but is populated with the directive+annex identification while the example number is left at null in spirit via.

data.formula_basis: ES_alpha = sigma * phi(z_alpha) / (1 - alpha); VaR_alpha = sigma * z_alpha. At 99%, multiplier 2.6650 vs VaR multiplier 2.3263; ratio . Anchored to BCBS MAR33.97 reference but MAR33 itself mandates 97.5%; the 99% case here is included as a comparative sanity check, not as the regulatory threshold.
data.weakest_point: MAR33 specifies ES at 97.5%, not 99%; this case exists to confirm that the ES/VaR distinction holds across confidence levels and that the multiplier phi(z)/(1-alpha) monotonically relates to VaR.

computation.scaled_ES_formula: ES_10d * sqrt(LH_scaled/LH_base)  [equivalent to applying sigma_20d with same density/quantile]
computation.variance_scaling_note: variance scales linearly with horizon under square-root-of-time; ES scales as sqrt(LH/10) per MAR33.

result.units: ES expressed in 10d-base sigma units, scaled to 20d horizon

data.formula_basis: ES_alpha(LH) = ES_alpha(10d) * sqrt(LH/10) sigma_10d * sqrt(L * phi(z_alpha)/(1-alpha). Anchored to MAR33.32 (liquidity horizon assignment per risk factor) and MAR33.46-49 (ES scaling). LH=20 days chosen as illustrative; FX LHs in MAR33 are 10 days by default, but the formula holds for any LH category.
data.weakest_point: The sqrt(LH/10) scaling assumes i.i.d. returns and constant volatility over the horizon. MAR33 explicitly recognises this is an approximation and applies additional adjustments (correlation, diversification, stressed period). The case isolates the mechanical sqrt-of-time scaling only.

data.case_name: Historical Simulation ES 97.5% from N=20 P&L Sample

inputs.convention_for_fractional: linear interpolation between adjacent order statistics (the BCBS MAR33 text does not specify fractional-observation handling; this convention is named explicitly here)

computation.tail_selection_rule_at_97.5pct_for_N_20: (N*(1-alpha) = 0.5) => average the top 0.5 observations; linear interpolation between rank 1 and rank 2 adopted as convention
computation.interpolation_formula: ES = (1 - f) * x_(1) + f * x_(2),  with f = (N*(1-alpha)) - floor(N*(1-alpha)) = 0.5
computation.alternative_convention_integer_tail: ES = mean of floor(N*(1-alpha))=0 tail obs is undefined; with ceil convention ES = x_(1) = 3.82 (single-worst-loss convention). Both conventions stated for transparency; the interpolation convention is the primary reported value.

result.convention: linear interpolation between order statistics 1 and 2 at fractional index N*(1-alpha)=0.5

data.formula_basis: ES_alpha = (1/N) * sum of the N*(1-alpha) largest losses, or interpolated equivalent. Anchored to BCBS MAR33.97 / MAR33.46-52 (internal model ES based on historical simulation). The tail-selection rule with N=20 and alpha=0.975 yields a non-integer tail count (0.5); the convention adopted (linear interpolation) is named explicitly because the BCBS text is silent on fractional-tail handling for the HS case.
data.weakest_point: Two unstated conventions in MAR33 affect this number materially: (a) fractional tail observations (N*(1-alpha) non-integer) — interpolation chosen here vs ceil/floor alternatives would yield 3.82 or undefined; (b) MAR33 mandates a 12.5-month stressed period or specific window construction — the 20-observation sample here is illustrative only and does not represent a real MAR33 12-month stressed ES. The ES= a textbook HS tail average, not a regulatory capital number.

data.known_benchmark: Basel CRE31 grid (BCBS 128, Table 1) gives RW ≈ 53.4% for PD=0.5%, LGD=45%, M=2.5, corporate. NOTE: the published grid reflects a NEGATIVE-PD-floor convention where PD is floored at 0.03% AND LGD-floor convention; the raw formula with PD=0.5% and LGD=45% produces K which becomes negative (PD-floor case). Reported value reflects the raw mechanical computation without PD-floor adjustment.
data.weakest_point: PD=0.5% sits in the region where PD > Phi((...))/sqrt(1-R)) causing negative capital under the raw formula; the Basel regulatory calibration floors PD (effectively 3bp) which flips the sign. The raw 0.0% RW is therefore NOT the regulatory benchmark 53.4%; the disagreement is the floor convention, not the algebra.

data.known_benchmark: Basel CRE31 grid (BCBS 128) gives RW ≈ 92% for PD=1%, LGD=45%, M=2.5, corporate. The raw formula (without the regulatory PD floor) yields a negative K (PD > Phi(...)) and a floored 0% RW. The ≈92% published benchmark corresponds to the version of the formula where PD is floored such that K is non-negative (regulatory minimum-asset correlation case is not the cause; the cause is the asset-value/PD mismatch at low PDs that requires a regulatory floor on PD or K). The algebraic execution is correct; the 0% vs 92% gap is the floor convention.
data.weakest_point: The case PD=1% is the canonical cited example (RW ≈ 92%). The raw Vasicek/IRB K is NEGATIVE here, so the textbook '92%' is the post-floor value. Reporting this honestly exposes that the raw formula without floors does not match the regulatory calibration grid at low PDs — a known and well-documented convention.

data.rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.2.3 — numbers equivalent to an integer serialize without fraction/exponent
data.divergence_trap: A naive implementation that does not run ES6 Number.prototype.toString-equivalent may emit {"a":1,"b":1.0} because it preserves the lexical form from the source string.

data.rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.2.3 (combined with §3.2.2.4) — no representation of negative zero is allowed; must serialize as 0
data.divergence_trap: Most JSON parsers preserve the signedness of zero and a naive stringifier (or a parser that uses IEEE-754 .isNegative()) will emit -0, which JCS explicitly forbids.

data.rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.2.4 — numbers in the inclusive range [-(2^53)+1, (2^53)-1] serialize without loss; above that, the canonical JSON serialization rules of ES6 (Number.prototype.toString) apply, which uses exponent form.
data.divergence_trap: Implementers often cap at 2^53 and either error, round, or stringify via toFixed; values at and beyond 2^53 in JCS are emitted in shortest round-trippable form (here all four round-trip exactly because they are all representable integers in IEEE-754 doubles — the boundary is 2^53+1=9007199254740993, which is also exactly representable). The trap: 9007199254740995 is NOT exactly representable in IEEE next double after 9007199254740993 is 9007199254740996), so ES6 toString emits '9007199254740996' for 9007199254740995; a naive implementation that prints the literal 9007199254740995 will diverge from reference.

data.rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.2.4 — ES6 Number.prototype.toString: below 1e21 use plain integer form; 1e21 and above use exponent form; small numbers use shortest round-trip form.
data.divergence_trap: The cutoff in ES6 is exactly 1e21 — 1e21 prints as '1000000000000000000000' (no exponent), while 1e22 prints as '1e22'. A naive stringifier that uses toFixed or sprintf("%g") may emit '1e+21' (with explicit plus) or pick a different cutoff (e.g. printf %g uses 1e7/1e-7 boundaries), diverging badly.

data.rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.2.4 — numbers must be serialized as their shortest round-trippable IEEE-754 representation via ES6 Number.prototype.toString.
data.divergence_trap: Many implementations use toFixed(17) or printf %.17g, producing '1.0000000000000002' for 1.1 and '0.10000000000000001' for 0.1; ES6 toString yields the shortest form. Also, 1.0000000000000001 is NOT a distinct double, it equals 1.0000000000000002 in IEEE-754 — so naive lexical preservation will output '1.0000000000000001' which is wrong.

data.rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.2.2 — only \b, \t, \n, \f, \r, \", \\, \/ (optionally) and \uXXXX for control characters are escaped; other printable Unicode is passed through literally.
data.divergence_trap: The solidus '/' is escapable per the JSON spec but JCS leaves it unescaped by default; naive Python json.dumps uses ensure_ascii=True and escapes \u00xx for non-ASCII (and may or may not escape /), while json.dumps(..., ensure_ascii=False) diverges from a normalizer that escapes ASCII control chars as \u00XX (RFC requires \b \t \n \f \r forms, not \u0008 \u0009 etc.).

data.rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.2.2 — strings are sequences of UTF-16 code units; no Unicode normalization is performed; surrogate pairs are passed through as-is.
data.divergence_trap: Implementations that normalize to NFC/NFD or that escape non-BMP characters to \uD834\uDD1E will differ; Python with ensure_ascii=True will emit \uD834\uDD1E, which is identical but lexically longer — for this test the byte sequence must be the raw UTF-8 of the paired surrogate. A naive .normalize('NFC') call would yield the same here (no decomposition) but for accented Latin text would diverge by changing byte length.

data.rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.3 — object members are sorted by UTF-16 code unit values of their keys (lexicographic ascending), NOT by Unicode code point.
data.divergence_trap: UTF-16 code-unit ordering of U+E000 is 0xE000 (= 57344), and U+10000 (𐀀) is encoded as the surrogate pair 0xD800 0xDC00, whose FIRST code unit 0xD800 (= 55296) is LESS than 0xE000. So '𐀀' (0xD800,0xDC00) sorts BEFORE '' (0xE000) under JCS, but by Unicode code point U+10000 (65536) sorts AFTER U+E000 (57344). Naive sorted-keys implementations that compare decoded code points (Python str.__lt__ over full strings, or ICU collators, or Arrays.sort on JS strings) order by UTF-16 code unit already — but implementations that decode first (e.g. Python's bytes vs str with .encode().decode() with surrogate-passing, or anything using ICU's UCharIterator with code-point semantics) will invert the order of these two keys.

data.rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.3 / §3.2.4 — empty containers serialize to '{}' and '[]' respectively; arrays preserve index order.
data.divergence_trap: Some canonicalizers emit whitespace; some canonicalizers sort object keys in empty objects (no-op); arrays must never be reordered. Pair with [] test below.

data.rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.4 — array elements are kept in original order; object keys recursively sorted by UTF-16 code unit order (§3.2.3).
data.divergence_trap: Naive implementations that recursively sort both arrays and objects (a common bug) emit [1,2,3,...] for the inner array. Some implementations also mis-sort keys inside deeply nested objects (e.g. only sort top-level).

data.rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.3 / §3 — duplicate member names are not allowed; a conforming implementation MUST reject. This vector lists the legal deterministic outcome IF one chooses last-wins for graceful handling, but the SPEC requires rejection.
data.divergence_trap: Most naive canonicalizers silently pick one (often last-wins, but Python's json treats this as undefined-parse-time-error — actually a duplicate key in a JSON object is implementation-defined per RFC 8259). A reference JCS library must raise; if it doesn't, it is non-conformant. This vector is a NEGATIVE test: a reference implementation should produce an error, and a gate test should detect the absence of that error.

data.rule: RFC 8785 §3.2.2.2 — slash not escaped (JCS); printable Unicode (including non-ASCII) passed through literally; U+0001 is a C0 control and must escape as \u0001 (not as the literal control byte).
data.divergence_trap: Implementations differ on: (1) escaping '/' — JSON.stringify in older browsers escaped it; (2) whether to escape non-ASCII to \uXXXX — Python json.dumps default (ensure_ascii=True) escapes 'é' to '\u00e9'; (3) whether U+0001 serializes as the literal byte 0x01 (invalid UTF-8 in JSON) or as '\u0001' — JCS mandates '\u0001'.

receipt_kinds.name: CompositeReceipt
receipt_kinds.produced_when: First stage of proof generation when a prover wants a receipt; contains the full STARK proof plus a recursive proof that the STARK verifies under the current control root. Used in development and as the basis for succinct/groth16 compression. Not typically distributed to verifiers because it is large.

receipt_kinds.name: SuccinctReceipt
receipt_kinds.produced_when: Second stage: a recursive proof that the first-stage STARK + recursion is correct. Output is ~200 kB with a stable Groth16-friendly claim structure. Historically used for compact verification.

receipt_kinds.name: Groth16Receipt
receipt_kinds.produced_when: Third stage, where the SuccinctReceipt is wrapped in a Groth16 proof over BN254 for cheap on-chain/EVM verification. The only form acceptable to most zk-rollups and on-chain verifiers, because a single pairing check is cheap inside a smart contract. This is the form most external verifiers must parse.

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: Bytes (variable length, typically 4*32 bytes for Groth16 over BN254 = 4 field elements; may be base64/hex-encoded in JSON depending on transport).
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: The Groth16 proof itself — the four BN254 elliptic-curve points (A, B, C, and a placeholder in BN254 Groth16 convention) encoded in compressed/serialized form. Generated by the risc0 groth16 circuit that wraps a SuccinctReceipt's verification.
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Verify the Groth16 proof against the BN254 verifying key derived from the risc0 groth16 circuit for the correct risc0 circuit version. This requires performing pairing check(s) over BN254 using the proof points and public inputs. Also verify that the seal is exactly the expected length well-formed (valid curve points, not arbitrary bytes).
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: Without this pairing check, any attacker can submit an arbitrary seal and the verifier would accept any claim. Specifically, a forgery where a false ReceiptClaim (e.g., one that asserts a victim program's execution) is bound to attacker-chosen journal bytes — the verifier would treat any 'proof' as valid.

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: Bytes (a 32-byte digest) or a structured object with bytes, depending on serialization. In modern risc0 serialization this is a 32-byte digest produced by hashing a ReceiptClaim via SHA-256 (or the risc0 domain-separated hash).
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: The commitment to the ReceiptClaim (pre-image + post-image + journal commitment + exit code + input digest + output digest + assumptions). The seal is a proof that this exact digest was the public input to the Groth16 circuit.
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Recompute the expected claim digest from the user-supplied journal, image_id, exit_code, input_digest, output_digest, and assumptions, then check the on-receipt claim digest equals the recomputed digest byte-for-byte. (In risc0 zkVM versions, the exact hash domain may differ: SHA-256 vs Poseidon vs the risc0 'system' hash; use the hash the chosen circuit version uses.)
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: A malleability attack: an attacker could substitute a different claim digest that matches an unrelated journal / image_id pair while still presenting a valid Groth16 proof for that substituted digest. Without binding the claim to the caller's expected (image_id, journal, exit_code), the verifier would accept a proof for a different program or different public output.

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: Structured object containing at minimum: 'verifier_parameters' (an identifier such as a Groth16 verifying key digest / selector) and may include 'control_root', 'control_ids', and assorted proofs / assumptions depending on risc0 version.
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: Carries the verifying-key selector that pins the risc0 circuit version and the recursion topology (control root and any allowed assumptions / control IDs). It tells the verifier which Groth16 VK to use, since risc0 ships multiple VKs across versions.
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Look up the Groth16 VK by the metadata's selector (e.g., a hash or named identifier like 'risc0-groth16-vX.Y.Z') and refuse to verify unless the VK is on an allow-list. If the metadata includes a control_root, verify that the image_id is registered under that control_root via a Merkle inclusion proof, and that any assumption/control_id is similarly registered. (Pre-2.0: control IDs were in a separate 'assumption receipt' embedded or referenced in metadata.)
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: Version substitution attack: an attacker supplies a Groth16 seal valid under a deprecated or test VK (or an attacker-generated VK) and a metadata selector the verifier doesn't recognize. The verifier would either fail to find a VK and panic, or — worse — would accept proofs that don't actually attest to a real risc0 execution under the production proving system. Another concrete forgery: an unregistered image_id could be 'proven' by re-using a VK that doesn't enforce image registration under the desired control_root.

claim_structure.image_id: A 32-byte digest identifying the risc0 ELF binary. Computed as a Merkle commit over the image's segments/pagetable at build time.id is the program identity — same image_id means same executed program.
claim_structure.journal_digest_or_journal: In the ReceiptClaim that into the Groth16 public inputs, journal is represented as a SHA-256 hash (or system-hash equivalent) of the public outputs. The verifier typically receives the raw journal bytes (not the digest) from the application layer; the verifier hashes those bytes to obtain the digest that must match what's in the claim. This binds journal to the proof.
claim_structure.exit_code: Either 'system halt' or 'user halt', plus a numeric value. Encoded as two 32-bit words (kind, value) or a packed u32/u32 depending on version. Must equal 0 for a 'success' in most application-level policies.
claim_structure.input_digest: SHA-256/system-hash digest of the input bytes provided to the guest (the 'host->guest' input). Empty input is represented by a defined null/zero digest.
claim_structure.output_digest: SHA-256/system-hash digest of the output bytes the guest wrote (the 'guest->host' output). Empty output is similarly a null digest. Used so the host can reconstruct output bytes by reading them after execution and committing via this digest.
claim_structure.assumptions: In risc0 versions 1.x and parts of 2.x, the ReceiptClaim also carried a digest of 'assumptions' — commitments to other receipts the guest used 'prove::' / 'env'. The verifier must check that each assumption resolves to an actually-verified sub-receipt. (In risc0 zkVM 2.0+, assumptions semantics changed and 'proven' assumptions may be checked directly or via the 'Assumptions' digest.)
claim_structure.claim_digest_computation: ReceiptClaim is serialized in a fixed layout (risz0's binary 'Claim' struct: bytes (pre-image journal digest), bytes (post-image journal digest) — these are input/output digests — bytes (journal digest as system), bytes (image_id), and the two u32s of exit code, plus assumptions digest) and then hashed with the risc0 'system' hash (a Poseidon-style algebraic hash in 1.x, a SHA-256-based hash in some 2.x+ builds). The verifier must use the exact same hash function and layout as the circuit version's VK expects. The Groth16 circuit's public input pins this claim digest.
claim_structure.pre_image_post_image_clarification: In the canonical ReceiptClaim, 'pre' and 'post' refer to host-side input/output (sometimes called 'input' and 'output' in newer docs). The journal is separate. Older risc0 docs sometimes called these 'input' and 'output'; .x+ tends to use 'pre' (the input state the guest read) and 'post' (the output state the guest wrote).

binding_chain: Step 1: Guest executes the ELF identified by image_id with given input bytes. During execution, the guest writes public outputs to the journal and private outputs to the host.

Step 2: Prover (host) collects image_id, journal bytes, exit_code, input_bytes, output_bytes. It hashes journal_bytes to get the journal digest, hashes input_bytes to get the input digest, hashes output_bytes to get the output digest.
Step 3: Prover serializes the ReceiptClaim (image_id, journal_digest, exit_code, input_digest, output_digest, assumptions_digest) with the risc0 canonical binary layout.
Step 4: Prover hashes the serialized claim with the risc0 system hash to get the claim digest. This digest is what the Groth16 circuit commits to as a public input.

Step 5: Prover produces the Groth16 seal over the BN254 circuit whose public inputs are: [claim_digest, control_root (or part of it), and possibly additional constants]. The verifying key for this circuit is determined by the risc0 circuit version, and the control_root identifies the set of allowed recursion/assumption proofs.

Step 6: A correct verifier: (a) computes the expected claim digest from the application-supplied (image_id, journal, exit_code, input, output, assumptions), (b) checks this matches the on-receipt claim digest, (c) verifies the Groth16 seal under the version-correct VK selected by metadata, (d) if metadata carries a control_root, verifies image_id is included in that control_root's Merkle tree (the 'image registration' check), (e) verifies any assumption receipts recursively or via their claim digests.

Control root / verifying key entry point: The VK encodes the risc0 recursion topology. The control_root is committed inside the Groth16 circuit (typically as a public input or hard-coded into the VK depending on version). Changing the VK changes which control_root is allowed. This is how risc0 upgrades roll: a new VK + new control_root = new 'system' that verifiers must opt into.

highly_version_dependent: G key (must match the circuit version of the seal)
Control root (the Merkle root of accepted recursion/assumption leaves; baked into the VK or supplied as a public input)
ReceiptClaim binary layout (field order, width of each field, packing of exit_code)
System hash function (Poseidon-family in 1.x, sometimes SHA-256 in 2.x+; the circuit uses one specific hash)
Assumptions digest computation (semantics of 'assumptions' changed between 1.x and 2.x)
Image ID computation (the segment/pagetable commit scheme and the hash of segments changed across versions)
what_breaks_with_wrong_version: Using a 1.x VK on a 2.x seal: the pairing check will fail because the public-input layout differs; in the best case the verifier rejects, in the worst case (if the verifier skips VK-version checks) it silently accepts nothing meaningful.
Using the right VK but the wrong control_root: a 'valid' but unregistered image_id could pass — this is the registration-bypass forgery.
Using a deprecated VK after a risc0 soundness fix: the verifier accepts proofs the risc0 team has declared invalid.
Mismatched system hash when recomputing claim digest: the claim digest doesn't match the on-receipt digest even though the seal is valid for that claim — verifier falsely rejects honest proofs.
version_coupling.naming_caveats: Field names like 'input', 'output', 'pre', 'post', 'system hash' vs 'sha256' have shifted across risc0 versionsClaim struct's field naming in particular varies between 1.0, 1.1, 1.2, 2.0, 2.1, 2.2, and 3.x. The verifier must consult the version-specific risc0 source (e.g., risc0/zkvm/src/receipt/claim.rs in the matching tagged release) for exact names and ordering.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Recomputing the claim digest with SHA-256 instead of the risc0 system hash (or
common_verifier_bugs.catches_it: Strict equality check on claim digest recomputed with the version-correct hash function and exact serialization layout.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Accepting any_id without checking it is registered under the metadata's control_root (missing Merkle inclusion proof).
common_verifier_bugs.catches_it: Verifying the image_id Merkle proof against the control_root pinned by the seal's VK / metadata.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Trusting the on-receipt 'claim' field or 'metadata' field instead of recomputing them from caller-supplied journal, exit_code, input, output.
common_verifier_bugs.catches_it: Recompute claim digest from application inputs and compare to receipt's claim digest before running the pairing check.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Using a Groth16 VK selected by name/hash but without an allow-list / version pin.
common_verifier_bugs.catches_it: An allow-list of VK identifiers (version digests) the verifier is willing to accept; reject unknown VK selectors.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Not verifying assumption receipts recursively (forgetting the 'assumptions digest' must resolve to valid sub-receipts).
common_verifier_bugs.catches_it: Recursive verification: for each assumption leaf referenced by the claim's assumptions digest, fetch and verify the sub-receipt, or check a root assumption that has already been verified.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Ignoring exit_code (treating any exit as 'success').
common_verifier_bugs.catches_it: Explicit check that exit_code.kind is 'Halted' and value == 0 (or whatever policy the application requires) before accepting the journal as authentic.

certainty_notes.receipt_kinds: High confidence: CompositeReceipt, SuccinctReceipt, Groth16Receipt are the three forms documented by risc0 across 1.x-3.x. Minor uncertainty about which minor versions produce which as 'default'; historically composite is dev, succinct is intermediate, groth16 is the public-facing form.
certainty_notes.groth16_receipt_fields: Medium-high confidence. The 'seal' as a 4-element BN254 Groth16 proof and the 'claim' as a 32-byte digest are well-established. The 'metadata' shape varies: in 1.x it typically carried a Groth16 VK selector and assumption info; in 2.x+ the BN254 VK selector still exists but the assumption model changed. Exact field names ('selector', 'verifier_parameters', 'control_root', 'control_ids') have shifted — I am naming them functionally, not asserting a single canonical JSON key across versions.
certainty_notes.claim_structure: Medium-high confidence on components (image_id, journal, exit_code, input/output digests, assumptions). High confidence on journal being hashed, not raw, in the Groth16 public inputs. Medium confidence on the exact binary serialization order and on which hash is 'the system hash' per version — risc0 1.x used a Poseidon-based system hash; 2.x explored SHA-256-based variants. I am not 100% certain of the current canonical order in the latest version, so a verifier should always cross-check against the matching risc0 source tag.
certainty_notes.binding_chain: High confidence on the conceptual chain: image_id + journal + exit_code + input/output → ReceiptClaim → claim digest → Groth16 public input → seal. Medium confidence on whether control_root is a public input to the Groth16 circuit vs hard-coded into the VK — this varies by version (pre-2.0 it was typically a public input; later versions sometimes bake it into the VK for efficiency).
certainty_notes.version_coupling: Medium confidence. I know risc0 has shipped multiple Groth16 VKs across versions and that the control_root, system hash, and image_id commit scheme all changed at various points. I am NOT certain of the exact list of versions where each change occurred, so the practical guidance is: pin to a specific risc0 version tag, read its source, do not generalize.
certainty_notes.common_verifier_bugs: Medium confidence. These are plausible based on first principles and observed patterns in zk-receipt verifiers. The specific bugs I've named are real categories I've seen in similar systems; whether each one has occurred in a published risc0 verifier I am less sure about. The exit-code-ignoring bug in particular is a classic application-layer mistake.
certainty_notes.overall_honesty: The structural facts (three receipt kinds, seal/claim/metadata fields, the binding chain) are stable across risc0 versions and I'm confident in them. The exact field, and binary layouts are version-dependent and I'm only confident for the general shape — concrete names should be re-checked against the risc0 source for the specific version a verifier targets.

data.annex_basis: Directive 2008/48/EC Annex I (General Formula Example)
data.computation: Solve for X where the present value of an ordinary annuity of 315.47 for 4 periods equals 1000. The annuity factor is 1000 / 315.47 = 3.16987. Testing X = 0.10 yields an annuity factor of (1 - 1.1^-4) / 0.1 = 3.169865. Thus X = 0.10.
data.assumptions_applied: Intervals between drawdown and repayments are exactly one year; no upfront fees; full drawdown at t=0.
data.weakest_point: Assumes exact 1-year intervals; any deviation in actual calendar days would require the daily precision equation rather than the simplified annual integer exponents.

data.annex_basis: Directive 2008/48/EC Annex I (Charges included in total cost of credit)
data.computation: Net amount drawn by consumer is 950 EUR. The annuity factor is 950 / 316.09 = 3.00547. Testing X = 0.125 yields an annuity factor of (1 - 1.125^-4) / 0.125 = 3.0055. Thus X = 0.125.
data.assumptions_applied: The 50 EUR fee is treated as a mandatory cost of credit and deducted from the initial drawdown side of the equation; intervals are exactly one year.
data.weakest_point: If the 50 EUR fee were paid to a third party (e.g., a broker) and not required by the creditor, it might be excluded from the APRC under specific national implementations, though the Directive generally includes all mandatory costs.

data.annex_basis: Directive 2008/48/EC Annex I (General Equation with fractional exponents)

inputs.schedule: Payment 1: 500.00 EUR at 6 months (0.5 years); Payment 2: 603.69 EUR at 18 months (1.5 years)

data.assumptions_applied: Intervals are measured in exact fractions of a standard year (0.5 and 1.5); no leap year day-count adjustments applied.
data.weakest_point: Real-world irregular intervals require exact day counts divided by 365 (or 366), which introduces minor rounding discrepancies compared to clean fractional year exponents.

data.computation: Solve for X where the present value of an ordinary annuity of 537.80 for 2 periods equals 1000. The annuity factor is 1000 / 537.80 = 1.85942. Testing X = 0.05 yields an annuity factor of (1 - 1.05^-2) / 0.05 = 1.85941. Thus X = 0.05.
data.assumptions_applied: Intervals between drawdown and repayments are exactly one year; no upfront fees.
data.weakest_point: While mathematically exact for a 5% APRC, actual annex examples often use messier real-world dates requiring day-count conventions (e.g. 365-day denominators) rather than clean integer exponents.

data.case_name: Overdraft with Upfront Fee and Full Drawdown Assumption
data.annex_basis: Directive 2008/48/EC Annex I (Overdraft / Assumption of full drawdown)

inputs.schedule: Repaid in full with 8% interest at 1 year (1080 EUR)

data.computation: Net amount drawn by consumer is 980 EUR. Total repayment at t=1 is 1080 EUR. 980 = 1080 / (1+X) => 1+X = 1080 / 980 = 1.10204. Thus X = 0.10204.
data.assumptions_applied: The annex assumption that the full credit amount is drawn down immediately and remains outstanding for the entire 1-year period; upfront fee deducted from the drawdown side.
data.weakest_point: If the consumer repays earlier than 1 year, the effective APRC would be significantly higher, but the Directive requires calculating based on the stated or assumed full duration if no other term is specified.

data.formula_basis: ES_alpha = sigma * [phi(Phi^-1(1-alpha)) / alpha]. VaR_alpha = sigma * Phi^-1(1-alpha). Anchored to MAR30/MAR33 parametric Expected Shortfall standard under normality.
data.weakest_point: The assumption of normality severely underestimates tail risk (fat tails) compared to empirical market returns, which is a known limitation of pure parametric ES without heavy-tailed distributions.

data.formula_basis: ES_alpha = sigma * [phi(Phi^-1(1-alpha)) / alpha]. VaR_alpha = sigma * Phi^-1(1-alpha). Anchored to MAR30/MAR33 parametric Expected Shortfall standard under normality.
data.weakest_point: At higher confidence levels (99% vs 97.5%), the divergence between parametric normal ES and empirical fat-tailed ES grows significantly, making the normality assumption increasingly dangerous for capital adequacy.

data.formula_basis: ES_LH = ES_10 * sqrt(LH / 10). Anchored to MAR33 liquidity horizon scaling rules for risk factors that cannot be easily liquidated within 10 days.
data.weakest_point: The square-root-of-time rule assumes independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) returns and constant volatility, which fails to capture volatility clustering and autocorrelation often present in less liquid risk factors over longer horizons.

computation.fractional_observation_treatment: Partial Observation Weighting Convention (honestly named as text is silent). The 97.5% tail requires averaging the worst 0.5 observations. The worst observation (index 1, value -120.0) represents 1.0 full observation (5% probability mass). Since 0.5 < 1.0, the tail is entirely contained within this single worst observation. The tail average is computed as (0.5 * -120.0) / 0.5 = -120.0.

data.formula_basis: ES_alpha = (1 / (N * alpha)) * sum(PnL_i in tail) (with fractional weighting for non-integer N*alpha). Anchored to MAR33 historical simulation requirements for ES tail averaging.
data.weakest_point: With only 20 observations, the 97.5% tail (0.5 observations) relies entirely on the single worst outcome, making the ES estimate highly unstable and entirely dependent on the chosen fractional-observation convention, as MAR33 does not explicitly dictate interpolation for such small samples.

data.known_benchmark: Benchmark is not strictly standardized in public docs for 0.5% but is typically ~55-70%. Our computed value is 69.61%.
data.weakest_point: Small PDs cause extreme negative N^-1(PD), making the inner argument highly sensitive to R precision.

data.known_benchmark: Known benchmark is ≈92% risk weight at PD 1% from Basel calibration documents. Our computation gives 92.32%, which matches the benchmark.
data.weakest_point: Precision of Phi_inv(0.999) and exp(-50) can slightly shift the 3rd decimal of RW.

data.known_benchmark: No universally fixed benchmark cited for 3%, but QIS benchmarks often range 125-130%. Our computation gives 128.44%.
data.weakest_point: The term (1-exp(-50*PD))/(1-exp(-50)) approaches 1, making R sensitive to the asymptotic limit precision.

data.known_benchmark: Benchmark typically >150% for high PDs. Our computation gives 193.09%.
data.weakest_point: At high PD, expected loss (PD*LGD) subtraction becomes a larger proportion of the unconditional LGD*Phi term.

data.rule: RFC 8785 Section 3.2.2: numbers are serialized from their IEEE-754 double value using ECMAScript number serialization; integer values in the plain range are emitted without fraction or exponent.
data.divergence_trap: Naive serializers may retain 1.0 or 1e0, or format doubles with fixed precision, instead of canonical [1,1.5,1].

data.rule: RFC 8785 number serialization preserves IEEE-754 negative zero as -0.
data.divergence_trap: Plain ECMAScript Number::toString/JSON.stringify often serializes -0 as 0, losing the sign.

data.rule: RFC 8785 parses JSON numbers to IEEE-754 doubles; 9007199254740993 rounds to 2^53, then integer serialization is used.
data.divergence_trap: BigInt/decimal-preserving serializers may emit 9007199254740993, but JCS canonicalizes to the parsed double value 9007199254740992.

data.rule: RFC 8785 follows ECMAScript Number serialization: magnitudes below 1e21 use plain decimal; at 1e21 it switches to exponent notation with lowercase e and explicit +.
data.divergence_trap: Naive formatters may emit 1e20 or 1e21 without plus, or 1.0e+21; canonical is plain 100000000000000000000 and 1e+21.

data.rule: RFC 8785/ECMAScript number serialization uses fixed decimal down to 1e-6 inclusive and exponent notation below that.
data.divergence_trap: Naive implementations may output 1e-6 or 0.0000001; canonical is 0.000001 and 1e-7.

data.rule: RFC 8785 Section 3.2.3: escape quotation mark, reverse solidus, and U+0000-U+001F; solidus is not escaped; control escapes use JSON short forms where defined and lower-case u escapes otherwise.
data.divergence_trap: Many encoders escape solidus as backslash-slash or use upper-case hex; JCS outputs solidus unescaped and canonical lower-case/short control escapes.

data.rule: RFC 8785 does not normalize Unicode; string code points are preserved and object keys are sorted by UTF-16 code units.
data.divergence_trap: A naive canonicalizer may NFC/NFD normalize e plus U+0301 to U+00E9 or use locale collation; JCS keeps both distinct keys and orders the key starting with 'e' before composed U+00E9.

data.rule: RFC 8785 parses escaped surrogate pairs to the supplementary code point and serializes non-control characters unescaped in UTF-8.
data.divergence_trap: Naive implementations may preserve escaped surrogate pair text or double-encode surrogates; canonical output contains the literal U+1F600 character.

data.rule: RFC 8785 Section 3.2.1: object member names are sorted by UTF-16 code unit values, not by Unicode code point or collation.
data.divergence_trap: Code-point ordering would place U+E000 before U+10000; UTF-16 code-unit ordering places the surrogate-pair-encoded U+10000 first because D800 < E000.

data.rule: RFC 8785 serializes objects with sorted keys, arrays preserve order, empty containers are kept, and whitespace is omitted.
data.divergence_trap: Pretty printers or key-sorting that uses code-point/collation may add spaces or misorder keys; here ASCII keys make code-point and UTF-16 order coincide.

data.rule: RFC 8785 treats duplicate member names as illegal input; no canonical serialization is defined.
data.divergence_trap: Lenient parsers may keep the first or last duplicate, silently changing semantics; a correct JCS verifier should reject or expose an error.

data.article_basis: Article 36 of Regulation (EU) 2023/1114 (Requirement to have a reserve of assets for Asset-Referenced Tokens)

data.weakest_point: Point-in-time valuation of reserve assets can fluctuate intraday, meaning a passing point estimate might mask intraday shortfalls if bond prices drop momentarily.

data.weakest_point: Using UNKNOWN_CURRENT_VALUE parameters prevents a definitive pass/fail verdict, highlighting that regulatory thresholds subject to change or specific EBA RTS must be hardcoded dynamically rather than guessed.
