receipt_kinds.produced_when: Default output of a risc0 zkVM execution session that spans multiple segments (or a single segment); consists of a chain/list of per-segment STARK receipts plus assumption receipts for any resolved `env::verify` calls, unified under a composite structure rather than a single proof object.
receipt_kinds.certainty: General/moderate — the existence of per-segment receipts chained via composite structure is a real risc0 design feature, but exact current struct naming may have shifted across versions.

receipt_kinds.produced_when: Produced by recursively compressing/folding the composite (multi-segment) STARK receipt into a single constant(ish)-size STARK proof via the recursion circuit ('lift' and 'join' recursion programs), so verification cost no longer scales with the number of segments.
receipt_kinds.certainty: Moderate — the lift/join recursion terminology reflects risc0's actual recursion-based aggregation design, though I am not fully certain of current exact program names.

receipt_kinds.produced_when: Produced by taking a succinct receipt and wrapping/compressing it one further step through a 'stark-to-snark' circuit that produces a Groth16 proof over the BN254 curve, giving small, constant-size, cheap-to-verify-on-chain (e.g. EVM) proofs — this is the form typically used for on-chain verification.
receipt_kinds.certainty: Moderate-high — the general architecture (STARK -> STARK recursion -> Groth16 wrapping over BN254 for on-chain verification) is a well-known risc0 design choice; exact circuit/tool naming (e.g. 'stark_verify' circuit) recalled with lower confidence.

groth16_receipt_fields.field: seal (Groth16 proof bytes: typically A, B, C group elements)
groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: Fixed-size byte array/struct encoding BN254 G1/G2 group elements (the standard Groth16 proof triple), possibly with a leading selector/version prefix byte(s) used by the on-chain verifier to pick a verifying key.
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: The actual zk-SNARK proof attesting that the wrapped STARK verification circuit accepted, i.e. that a valid succinct receipt existed for the claimed computation.
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Run the Groth16 pairing check e(A,B) = e(alpha,beta)*e(C,gamma)^-1*... against the fixed verifying key for the corresponding circuit version, with the public inputs derived from the claim digest.
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: If the pairing check itself is skipped or short-circuited, any seal bytes (including garbage or a proof for an unrelated statement) would be accepted, letting an attacker submit a forged claim of arbitrary program execution and output.

groth16_receipt_fields.field: claim / journal digest encoded as public input(s)
groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: One or more field elements (BN254 scalar field elements) derived from hashing/packing the ReceiptClaim digest (or journal digest + image ID digest) into the Groth16 circuit's public input format.
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: Binds the SNARK proof to a specific claim (specific program image, specific journal/output, specific exit code) rather than being a proof of 'some computation happened.'
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Recompute the expected public input(s) independently from the claim the verifier is checking against (its own copy of image ID + journal bytes + exit code), and compare bit-for-bit/field-element-for-field-element against what's fed into the pairing check — never trust public inputs supplied alongside the seal without recomputation.
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: If the verifier accepts attacker-supplied public inputs instead of recomputing them from the claim it actually cares about, an attacker can pair a valid seal for claim A with public inputs claiming to be for claim B, causing the verifier to believe an unrelated (possibly malicious) program's output was produced by the expected image.

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: A fixed-size digest (commonly a 256-bit / 32-byte hash, sometimes represented as multiple field-sized words) identifying the compiled guest program (its RISC-V ELF/binary content, effectively a commitment to the exact code that ran).
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: Tells the verifier WHICH program produced the journal — i.e., that the specific known/audited guest binary was executed, not some arbitrary code.
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Compare the image ID embedded in (or derivable from) the claim against the expected/whitelisted image ID for the application in question, exactly, before trusting the journal contents.
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: If the verifier checks that 'some valid receipt exists' but never pins down which image ID it corresponds to, an attacker can get a legitimately-proven receipt for a DIFFERENT (attacker-controlled) guest program and pass off its journal as if it came from the expected, trusted program.

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: A digest (hash) of the journal bytes — the public output data the guest program committed to via `env::commit`.
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: Commits to the actual output/result the program produced, without requiring the full (potentially large) journal bytes to be part of the SNARK's public inputs directly.
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Recompute the digest of the journal bytes it has received out-of-band and compare against the journal digest embedded in the claim/public inputs, ensuring the journal the verifier is reading was really the one committed to inside the proof.
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: If the verifier trusts journal bytes handed to it separately from the receipt without re-hashing and comparing to the committed digest, an attacker can present a valid proof for one journal digest alongside a swapped, more favorable set of journal bytes.

groth16_receipt_fields.field: exit code (system + user exit code pair)
groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: A small enum/struct value, e.g. a pair distinguishing normal halt vs fault vs 'system split' (used internally for segmentation) vs paused, plus a user-supplied sub-code on normal halt.
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: Encodes how/why the guest program terminated — whether it was a clean successful halt with a given user code, or an abnormal termination.
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Confirm the exit code indicates a legitimate, expected successful halt (and, if the application semantics depend on the specific user exit sub-code, check that value too) rather than accepting receipts for faulted or paused executions as if they were successful.
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: If a verifier accepts any exit code as valid, a guest program that faulted partway through (potentially with attacker-influenced partial/garbage journal state, depending on implementation) or that used a 'paused' continuation state could be misinterpreted as a completed, trustworthy computation.

groth16_receipt_fields.field: control root / control ID (recursion verifying-key commitment)
groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: A digest or small set of digests identifying which version of risc0's recursion/aggregation circuits (and ultimately which Groth16 verifying key) were used to produce this receipt.
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: Pins the receipt to a specific trusted circuit-version lineage, since the STARK-to-STARK recursion and STARK-to-SNARK wrapping circuits are versioned artifacts of the risc0 toolchain, not the guest program itself.
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Verify that the control root/ID embedded in or implied by the receipt matches one of the verifier's allow-listed, trusted control roots for the version(s) of risc0 it supports, and that the Groth16 verifying key used for the pairing check corresponds to that same version.
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: If the verifier does not pin the control root/ID to a known-good set, an attacker could exploit a receipt generated by a deprecated, buggy, or maliciously modified version of the recursion circuits (if such a version's verifying key were somehow substitutable) to get proofs accepted for computations that were never actually correctly proven under the intended circuit.

components: pre_state_digest / image ID — commitment to the guest program binary/method being executed (and, in continuation contexts, the starting machine state)

post_state_digest — commitment to the ending machine state after execution (used internally across segment boundaries in composite receipts; often not directly meaningful to an application-level verifier beyond confirming a clean halt)
exit_code — system exit code (e.g., Halted, Paused, SystemSplit, Fault) paired with a user-defined sub-code on Halted
input digest — a commitment to any input data the guest was configured with (used in some verification flows; may be a zero/empty digest when unused)

output digest / journal digest — commitment to the journal bytes (public output) the guest committed via `env::commit`, typically wrapped inside an 'Output' structure that may also include an assumptions digest for composite receipts
claim_structure.claim_digest_computation: The ReceiptClaim struct's fields are serialized into a fixed structure and hashed (using risc0's chosen hash, historically SHA-256-based tagged hashing for its internal Merkle/struct-hash scheme) to produce a single claim digest; this digest is what ultimately gets bound into the recursion/Groth16 circuit's public inputs, rather than the individual fields being passed through separately.
claim_structure.certainty: Moderate — the conceptual shape (pre-state/image commitment, post-state, exit code, input/output digests folded into one struct that gets hashed) matches risc0's actual ReceiptClaim design, but exact current field names (e.g., whether it's literally called 'pre_state_digest' vs something else in the current source) and the precise tagged-hash construction are not recalled with high confidence and may have changed across major versions.

binding_chain: Step 1: The guest program executes and calls `env::commit(&data)`, and the zkVM serializes and hashes this data into the journal digest as part of the execution trace.

Step 2: At segment-proof time, the STARK circuit constrains that the claimed journal digest (and image ID, exit code, etc.) is consistent with the actual machine execution trace being proven — this is where 'journal bytes' become cryptographically tied to 'claim digest' via the per-segment STARK proof(s).

Step 3: Composite (multi-segment) receipts are aggregated via the recursion circuit(s) (lift/join), which prove 'these per-segment claims chain together into one overall claim' without re-executing the original computation, producing a succinct receipt whose single claim digest still traces back to the same journal/image/exit-code commitments.

Step 4: The succinct receipt's STARK proof and its claim digest are fed into the stark-to-snark wrapping circuit, which is itself a fixed circuit whose correctness (and whose verifying key) depends on a specific 'control root'/control ID identifying that exact version of the recursion verifier being wrapped.

Step 5: The stark-to-snark circuit outputs public inputs for the Groth16 proof that encode (typically as one or more BN254 field elements) the claim digest (or a further hash/packing of it) plus the control root, so the Groth16 seal is only valid for that specific (claim digest, control root) pairing.

Step 6: An on-chain or off-chain verifier holding the fixed Groth16 verifying key (which is itself tied to the control root's circuit version) recomputes the expected public inputs from its own trusted image ID + journal bytes + exit code + expected control root, and checks the Groth16 pairing equation against the seal — if it passes, the entire chain from journal bytes up through the SNARK is bound together.

Moderate — the high-level 'commit -> STARK -> recursion -> wrap -> SNARK public inputs -> pairing check' pipeline reflects real risc0 architecture, but the precise point(s) at which control root enters the public inputs vs. is hardcoded into the verifying key, and the exact field-packing scheme, are recalled at lower confidence and could differ from the current implementation.

circuit_version_dependent_parameters: The Groth16 verifying key (alpha/beta/gamma/delta group elements and IC coefficients) is tied to one specific compiled stark-to-snark circuit, which changes whenever risc0 updates its recursion/wrapping circuits.

The control root / set of control IDs (identifying which recursion programs — lift, join, resolve, identity, etc. — are considered valid) changes across risc0 releases as the recursion circuit set is revised or extended.

The STARK proof system parameters used inside the succinct/composite receipts (field, hash function, FRI parameters) for the base zkVM circuit are also version-pinned, though these matter less to a pure Groth16-receipt verifier since that layer is already compressed away by the wrapping step.
version_coupling.what_breaks_with_mismatched_version: If a verifier uses an outdated or wrong verifying key for a receipt produced by a newer (or differently-configured) risc0 toolchain version, Groth16 pairing verification will simply fail (proof rejected) in the honest-mismatch case — but the more dangerous failure mode is a verifier that accepts an OLD, deprecated verifying key/control root pair whose validity should have been revoked (e.g., because that old circuit had a discovered bug), allowing receipts crafted against the deprecated, faulty circuit to be accepted as if they were current.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Recomputing the claim digest with an out-of-date field ordering/serialization or the wrong hash tag, or forgetting to include one field of the claim entirely (e.g. omitting exit code) when constructing the expected digest.
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches_it: Cross-check the verifier's claim-digest computation against reference test vectors covering all claim fields, including at least one test case where a single field changes and the digest must change too.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Trusting an image ID or journal bytes passed alongside the receipt without recomputing/comparing them against what's actually bound into the proof's public inputs.
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches_it: A test where the accompanying (out-of-band) journal bytes or image ID are deliberately mismatched from the ones baked into a valid seal, confirming the verifier rejects rather than silently trusting the mismatched side channel.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Accepting any exit code (including Fault or Paused) as if it were a successful Halt, because the verifier only checks 'proof verifies' and not 'the underlying claim represents a completed successful execution.'
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches_it: A test receipt with a non-Halted exit code (still a validly-provable claim about a real, if unsuccessful/incomplete, execution) that the verifier must explicitly reject at the application layer.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Hardcoding or accepting a verifying key/control root without pinning it to an explicit allow-list, so a receipt generated under an old/deprecated or unofficial circuit build silently verifies.
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches_it: A test that swaps in a receipt produced (or simulated) under a known-deprecated control root and confirms the verifier rejects it due to the allow-list check, independent of whether the Groth16 pairing itself would pass.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Off-by-one or endianness errors when packing the claim digest into BN254 scalar-field public input elements (since a 256-bit digest doesn't fit directly into one BN254 scalar field element without truncation/splitting), causing the verifier to silently check a truncated or shifted version of the intended digest.
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches_it: Test vectors with claim digests near field-size boundaries or with specific bit patterns in the top bits, confirming the packing/truncation the verifier applies exactly matches the packing used at proof-generation time.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Reusing or caching a verification result keyed only on the seal bytes without also keying on the (claim digest, control root) pair, so a seal that is legitimately reused across contexts (if the system allows receipt reuse) is treated as valid for a DIFFERENT claim than the one it actually attests to.
common_verifier_bugs.check_that_catches_it: A test that submits the same seal bytes alongside two different claimed (image ID, journal) pairs and confirms the verifier only accepts the one whose recomputed public inputs actually match the seal.

certainty_notes.receipt_kinds: Moderate confidence on the composite -> succinct -> groth16 progression and its general purpose (cost reduction, on-chain verification); low-moderate confidence on exact current struct/program names.
certainty_notes.groth16_receipt_fields: The conceptual role of each field (seal, public inputs, image ID, journal digest, exit code, control root) is drawn from general risc0 architecture knowledge; exact byte layouts, field orderings, and current struct/serialization names are NOT verified against source and should be treated as approximate rather than exact.
certainty_notes.claim_structure: Moderate confidence on the conceptual claim components (image/pre-state, post-state, exit code, input/output digests folded into one hashed struct); low confidence on exact current field names and the precise tagged-hash algorithm details.
certainty_notes.binding_chain: Moderate confidence on the high-level pipeline shape; low-moderate confidence on exactly where/how control root enters the public inputs versus being baked into the verifying key, and on the precise field-packing of a 256-bit digest into BN254 scalars.
certainty_notes.version_coupling: Moderate-high confidence on the general principle that verifying key and control root/IDs are version-pinned artifacts that must be matched; low confidence on specifics of how risc0 currently manages/publishes/rotates these across releases.
certainty_notes.common_verifier_bugs: These are constructed from general zk-SNARK/zkVM verifier-implementation reasoning (a defect-pattern library applicable to STARK/SNARK-wrapped verification systems generally) rather than recalled from specific documented risc0 CVEs or incident reports; I am not confidently aware of specific historical risc0 verifier bugs matching each entry, and these should be read as plausible risk classes to test for, not confirmed historical incidents.
certainty_notes.overall: This document reflects general/moderate-confidence architectural knowledge of the risc0 zkVM proof system as of its v1.x-era public design, not a verified read of the current source code or documentation; several field names, exact digest/serialization schemes, and version-specific details are flagged as uncertain rather than asserted, per the task's instructions.

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: struct Groth16Seal { a: G1Affine, b: G2Affine, c: G1Affine, public_inputs: Vec<Fr> } or serialized proof bytes
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: The Groth16 proof over BN254 attesting to validity of the underlying STARK
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Run Groth16 verify with the hardcoded verifying key (version-specific) and the claim digest as the sole public input
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: Verifier accepts any Groth16 proof from the same circuit regardless of which claim it binds to; attacker reuses a proof for a different (benign) program to forge acceptance of a malicious one

groth16_receipt_fields.type_shape: ReceiptClaim { pre: Digest, post: Digest, exit_code: ExitCode, input: MaybeDigest, output: MaybeDigest }
groth16_receipt_fields.meaning: The structured statement: what program ran, what input/output, what exit status
groth16_receipt_fields.verifier_must_check: Compute claim.digest(), ensure it matches the public_inputs of the seal; check claim.image_id (derived from post-state / control root) equals the expected guest image ID; check claim.exit_code == 0
groth16_receipt_fields.failure_if_skipped: Verifier reads journal but ignores image_id binding; accepts a proof from a different guest program that happens to produce the same journal structure — cross-program confusion forgery

components.pre: Digest — VM state before execution (typically all zeros / initial state)
components.post: Digest — VM state after execution; encodes the image ID and final memory/PC
components.exit_code: ExitCode enum — Halted(0) for success, Paused, or Failed
components.input: MaybeDigest — None or hash of the guest input (committed via sys_read)
components.output: MaybeDigest — None or hash of the journal (committed via sys_write to output)

claim_structure.journal_binding: Guest writes to journal via syscalls; at end, journal bytes are hashed (SHA-256) to produce the output digest stored in claim.output
claim_structure.claim_digest_computation:
claim.digest() = SHA-256(domain_separated_encoding(pre |post
exit_code
input
| output)); the exact domain separator may vary across v1.x-3.x
claim_structure.image_id_note: image_id is not a separate field in ReceiptClaim; it is extracted from the post state digest which commits to the control root + ELF. Field names: post.state.contains(image_id, control_id_root)

binding_chain: 1. Guest execution produces journal bytes (public outputs)
2. Journal bytes → SHA-256 → output digest (stored in claim.output)
3. ReceiptClaim constructed with pre, post, exit_code, input, output
4. claim.digest() = hash(claim) → this is the public statement the STARK proves
5. STARK prover produces SuccinctReceipt.seal attesting that a trace exists whose commitment opens to claim.digest()
6. Groth16 prover takes the STARK verification circuit as witness; produces Groth16Seal with claim.digest() as the circuit's public input
7. Verifier: Groth16 verify(seal, vk, claim.digest()) — if passes, the claim is trustlessly established
8. Control root enters at step 5: it is hardcoded into the STARK verifier circuit; the Groth16 VK corresponds to that circuit version

circuit_version_dependent_parts: Groth16 verifying key (VK) — regenerated if STARK-to-Groth16 circuit constraints change (e.g., field arithmetic, hash function changes)
Control root / control IDs — change if the RISC-V instruction set implementation, builtins, or STARK parameters (trace length, colinearity) change
Image ID derivation — depends on control root; same ELF → different image_id if control root differs
version_coupling.what_breaks_with_wrong_version: Using a VK from version N to verify a proof from version M: verification fails (proof rejected) if constraints differ; if an old VK is accidentally accepted for a new circuit, the algebraic relation is broken and the proof may verify for an invalid trace (if the circuit had a bug fixed in the new version). Using wrong control root: image_id mismatch causes verifier to reject, OR if verifier doesn't pin image_id, accepts a program compiled under a different (possibly insecure) control root.

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Verifier deserializes seal and checks Groth16 pairing but hardcodes public input to 0 or ignores claim.digest()
common_verifier_bugs.check: Compute claim.digest() from the received claim struct and pass it as the exact public input vector to the Groth16 verifier

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Verifier checks claim.output digest but does not compare claim.image_id (from post state) against the expected guest's image_id
common_verifier_bugs.check: Extract image_id from claim.post (or claim.image_id() helper) and assert equality with the trusted compile-time constant

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Verifier does not check claim.exit_code == Halted(0), accepting proofs of failed or paused executions
common_verifier_bugs.check: Assert claim.exit_code indicates successful termination before using journal

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Verifier accepts a SuccinctReceipt directly when the protocol expects Groth16Receipt, skipping the Groth16 check entirely
common_verifier_bugs.check: Enforce receipt type at the protocol level; only deserialize as Groth16Receipt when that is the expected variant

common_verifier_bugs.bug: Verifier re-hashes journal bytes using a different hash (e.g., Keccak instead of SHA-256) than the risc0 circuit uses
common_verifier_bugs.check: Use the exact hash function and domain separation that the guest's sys_write syscall commits to (SHA-256 in v1.x-3.x)

data.case_name: Case 1 — Single direct ownership (≥50% threshold, one path only)
data.computation:
Direct path: A → C, A owns 55% of C.

OFAC 50 Percent Rule: an entity is blocked if one or more blocked persons own 50% or more in the aggregate, directly or indirectly.

Direct ownership by blocked person A = 55%.
No intermediaries. No indirect paths.

Aggregate blocked ownership of C = 55%.

Since 55% ≥ 50%, C is blocked.

This is the simplest case: a single direct edge from a blocked person to the target, above the threshold.
data.guidance_basis: OFAC 50 Percent Rule: entities owned 50% or more, directly or indirectly, in the aggregate by one or more blocked persons are themselves blocked. See OFAC FAQ 398 and related guidance on the 50 Percent Rule. This case is a straightforward direct-ownership example.
data.weakest_point: This case is intentionally trivial and the result is unambiguous. The only uncertainty is whether the specific ownership percentage (55%) or entity labels match any published OFAC example; I believe OFAC has published simple direct-ownership illustrations, but I do not recall a specific example with these exact numbers.

data.case_name: Case 2 — Convergent graph: multiple paths to same target, mixed blocked/non-blocked intermediaries (interpretation-dependent outcome)
data.computation:
Step 1 — Identify blocked entities:
  - A is directly blocked (given).
  - B1: A owns 50% of B1. A is blocked. Blocked ownership of B1 = 50%. Since 50% ≥ 50%, B1 IS BLOCKED.
  - B2: A owns 40% of B2. No other blocked person owns B2. Blocked ownership of B2 = 40%. Since 40% < 50%, B2 is NOT blocked.
  - C: compute below.

Step 2 — Compute aggregate blocked ownership of C:

  Path 1 (direct): A → C, 10%.
    A is blocked, direct ownership = 10%.

  Path 2 (through blocked intermediary B1): A → B1 → C.
    B1 is blocked (A owns 50% of B1).
    B1 owns 30% of C.
    Since B1 is a blocked person, B1's 30% ownership of C is counted as blocked ownership.
    Attribution to A: A, as the 50% owner of B1, is attributed B1's 30% ownership of C (full attribution through a blocked ≥50% intermediary).
    Contribution = 30%.

  Path 3 (through non-blocked intermediary B2): A → B2 → C.
    B2 is NOT blocked (A owns only 40%, below 50%).
    A's indirect ownership through B2 = A's ownership of B2 × B2's ownership of C = 40% × 25% = 10%.
    (Multiplicative treatment applies through non-blocked intermediaries.)
    Contribution = 10%.

  Total aggregate blocked ownership of C = 10% + 30% + 10% = 50%.

  Since 50% ≥ 50%, C IS BLOCKED.

Step 3 — Compare with the alternative (multiplicative-through-all) treatment:
  If one incorrectly applied multiplicative attribution through ALL intermediaries (including blocked ones):
    A via B1 = 50% × 30% = 15% (instead of full 30%).
    A via B2 = 40% × 25% = 10%.
    A direct = 10%.
    Total = 10% + 15% + 10% = 35%.
    Under this incorrect treatment, C would NOT be blocked (35% < 50%).
  This case is designed to expose that error: the outcome flips entirely depending on whether blocked intermediaries' full ownership is attributed or only the multiplicative share is counted.

Ownership consistency check:
  Total ownership of C accounted for: 10% (A direct) + 30% (B1) + 25% (B2) = 65%.
  Remaining 35% is owned by non-blocked persons not modeled here.
  No overlap; no double-counting.
data.blocked_verdicts: C is BLOCKED under the full-attribution-through-blocked-intermediaries approach (aggregate blocked ownership = 50%, which meets the threshold). Under an incorrect multiplicative-through-all approach, C would NOT be blocked (35%).
data.guidance_basis: OFAC 50 Percent Rule (FAQ 398 and related guidance): entities 50% or more owned, directly or indirectly, in the aggregate by one or more blocked persons are blocked. The rule applies to 'directly or indirectly' owned entities. The critical interpretive question — how indirect ownership through a majority-owned (and thus blocked) intermediary is treated — is the load-bearing rule. My computation applies the approach that a blocked intermediary's ownership of a downstream entity is counted as blocked ownership (because the intermediary itself is a blocked person), and that the upstream blocked owner is attributed that full ownership (full attribution), as opposed to only the multiplicative share. I am NOT 100% certain this full-attribution interpretation is the precise position OFAC has taken in every published statement; I have seen arguments both for full attribution and for strict multiplication. The case is structured so that the two approaches yield opposite verdicts, exposing the interpretive gap.
data.weakest_point: The single most uncertain point is the exact OFAC treatment of indirect ownership through a majority-owned (and thus blocked) intermediary: whether the intermediary's full downstream ownership is attributed to the upstream blocked owner (full attribution, 30% here) or only the multiplicative share is counted (50% × 30% = 15% here). My computation uses full attribution, which yields a blocked verdict for C at exactly 50%; multiplicative would yield 35% and not block C. I am not certain which OFAC has officially prescribed, and this is the key interpretive risk in this case and in the broader analysis.

data.case_name: Case 3 — Second convergent graph: two intermediaries, one blocked one not, opposite outcome under the two interpretations
data.computation:
Step 1 — Identify blocked entities:
  - D is directly blocked (given).
  - F: D owns 55% of F. D is blocked. Blocked ownership of F = 55%. Since 55% ≥ 50%, F IS BLOCKED.
  - G: D owns 35% of G. No other blocked person owns G. Blocked ownership of G = 35%. Since 35% < 50%, G is NOT blocked.
  - E: compute below.

Step 2 — Compute aggregate blocked ownership of E:

  Path 1 (direct): D → E, 20%.
    D is blocked, direct ownership = 20%.

  Path 2 (through blocked intermediary F): D → F → E.
    F is blocked (D owns 55% ≥ 50%).
    F owns 35% of E.
    Since F is a blocked person, F's 35% ownership of E is counted as blocked ownership.
    Attribution to D: D, as the 55% owner of F, is attributed F's 35% ownership of E (full attribution).
    Contribution = 35%.

  Path 3 (through non-blocked intermediary G): D → G → E.
    G is NOT blocked (D owns only 35%).
    D's indirect ownership through G = D's ownership of G × G's ownership of E = 35% × 20% = 7%.
    (Multiplicative treatment through non-blocked intermediary.)
    Contribution = 7%.

  Total aggregate blocked ownership of E = 20% + 35% + 7% = 62%.

  Since 62% ≥ 50%, E IS BLOCKED.

Step 3 — Compare with multiplicative-through-all:
  D via F = 55% × 35% = 19.25%.
  D via G = 35% × 20% = 7%.
  D direct = 20%.
  Total = 20% + 19.25% + 7% = 46.25%.
  Under multiplicative, E would NOT be blocked (46.25% < 50%).

  The two approaches yield opposite verdicts: 62% (blocked) vs. 46.25% (not blocked).

Ownership consistency check:
  Total ownership of E accounted for: 20% (D direct) + 35% (F) + 20% (G) = 75%.
  Remaining 25% owned by non-blocked persons not modeled.
  No double-counting.
data.blocked_verdicts: E is BLOCKED under the full-attribution-through-blocked-intermediaries approach (aggregate blocked ownership = 62% ≥ 50%). Under multiplicative-through-all, E would NOT be blocked (46.25%).
data.guidance_basis: OFAC 50 Percent Rule (FAQ 398 and related guidance). Same interpretive question as Case 2: whether a blocked intermediary's full downstream ownership is attributed to the upstream blocked owner, or only the multiplicative share. The structure is identical in form to Case 2 but with different numbers, yielding a different margin (62% blocked vs. 46.25% not).
data.weakest_point: Same interpretive uncertainty as Case 2: the precise OFAC treatment of indirect ownership through a majority-owned (blocked) intermediary — full attribution vs. multiplicative — is the load-bearing rule and the point on which I am least certain. This case is a second convergent graph (meeting the prompt's requirement of at least two) and is structured to show the opposite outcome under the two interpretations.

data.case_name: Case 4 — Chain through a majority-owned intermediary (required: ≥1 such case)
data.computation:
Step 1 — Identify blocked entities:
  - A is directly blocked (given).
  - B: A owns 51% of B. A is blocked. Blocked ownership of B = 51%. Since 51% ≥ 50%, B IS BLOCKED.
  - C: compute below.

Step 2 — Compute aggregate blocked ownership of C:

  Path 1 (direct): A → C, 10%.
    A is blocked, direct ownership = 10%.

  Path 2 (through majority-owned intermediary B): A → B → C.
    B is blocked (A owns 51% ≥ 50%).
    B owns 45% of C.
    Since B is a blocked person, B's 45% ownership of C is counted as blocked ownership.
    Attribution to A: A, as the 51% owner of B, is attributed B's 45% ownership of C (full attribution through a blocked ≥50% intermediary).
    Contribution = 45%.

  Total aggregate blocked ownership of C = 10% + 45% = 55%.

  Since 55% ≥ 50%, C IS BLOCKED.

Step 3 — Compare with multiplicative-through-all (incorrect):
  A via B = 51% × 45% = 22.95%.
  A direct = 10%.
  Total = 32.95%.
  Under multiplicative, C would NOT be blocked (32.95% < 50%).

  This case illustrates the required scenario: a chain through a majority-owned intermediary. The intermediate entity B is itself blocked because a blocked person (A) owns 51% of it. B's downstream ownership of C (45%) is then attributed, yielding a blocked verdict for C at 55%. Under strict multiplication, the same chain yields only 32.95% and C would not be blocked.

Ownership consistency check:
  Total ownership of C: 10% (A direct) + 45% (B) = 55%.
  Remaining 45% owned by non-blocked persons not modeled.
  No double-counting: B's 45% is counted once as blocked ownership; it is not separately multiplied through to A.
data.blocked_verdicts: C is BLOCKED under the full-attribution-through-blocked-intermediaries approach (B is blocked, B's 45% of C + A's 10% direct = 55% ≥ 50%). Under multiplicative-through-all, C would NOT be blocked (32.95%).
data.guidance_basis: OFAC 50 Percent Rule (FAQ 398 and related guidance). This case specifically illustrates the chain-through-majority-owned-intermediary scenario required by the prompt. The key rule applied: when an intermediary is itself blocked (≥50% owned by blocked persons), its ownership of a downstream entity is counted as blocked ownership, and the upstream blocked owner is attributed that ownership. The alternative (multiplicative-through-all) yields a different result.
data.weakest_point: Same interpretive uncertainty as Cases 2 and 3: whether OFAC's guidance prescribes full attribution of a blocked intermediary's downstream ownership to the upstream blocked owners, or only multiplicative attribution. My computation applies full attribution, yielding a blocked verdict for C at 55%; multiplicative yields 32.95% and not blocked. I am not certain which treatment OFAC has officially prescribed.

data.case_name: Case 5 — Two blocked owners (A and D), convergent paths through multiple intermediaries, interpretation-dependent outcome
data.computation:
Step 1 — Identify blocked entities:
  - A and D are directly blocked (given).
  - B1: A owns 51% of B1. A is blocked. Blocked ownership of B1 = 51%. Since 51% ≥ 50%, B1 IS BLOCKED.
  - B2: D owns 51% of B2. D is blocked. Blocked ownership of B2 = 51%. Since 51% ≥ 50%, B2 IS BLOCKED.
  - B3: A owns 30% of B3. No other blocked person owns B3. Blocked ownership of B3 = 30%. Since 30% < 50%, B3 is NOT blocked.
  - B4: D owns 25% of B4. No other blocked person owns B4. Blocked ownership of B4 = 25%. Since 25% < 50%, B4 is NOT blocked.
  - C: compute below.

Step 2 — Compute aggregate blocked ownership of C:

  Blocked persons: A and D.

  A's contributions:
    A direct → C: 10%.
    A via B1 (blocked intermediary): B1 owns 20% of C. B1 is blocked, so B1's 20% is blocked ownership. A, as 51% owner of B1, is attributed B1's full 20% (full attribution). Contribution = 20%.
    A via B3 (non-blocked intermediary): 30% × 12% = 3.6% (multiplicative).
    A's total = 10% + 20% + 3.6% = 33.6%.

  D's contributions:
    D direct → C: 10%.
    D via B2 (blocked intermediary): B2 owns 15% of C. B2 is blocked, so B2's 15% is blocked ownership. D, as 51% owner of B2, is attributed B2's full 15% (full attribution). Contribution = 15%.
    D via B4 (non-blocked intermediary): 25% × 8% = 2% (multiplicative).
    D's total = 10% + 15% + 2% = 27%.

  Aggregate blocked ownership of C = A's total + D's total = 33.6% + 27% = 60.6%.

  Since 60.6% ≥ 50%, C IS BLOCKED.

Step 3 — Compare with multiplicative-through-all (incorrect):
  A via B1 = 51% × 20% = 10.2% (instead of 20%).
  D via B2 = 51% × 15% = 7.65% (instead of 15%).
  A via B3 = 30% × 12% = 3.6% (same).
  D via B4 = 25% × 8% = 2% (same).
  A direct = 10%, D direct = 10%.
  Total = 10% + 10% + 10.2% + 7.65% + 3.6% + 2% = 43.45%.
  Under multiplicative, C would NOT be blocked (43.45% < 50%).

  The two approaches yield opposite verdicts: 60.6% (blocked) vs. 43.45% (not blocked).

Ownership consistency check:
  Total ownership of C accounted for:
    A direct: 10%
    D direct: 10%
    B1: 20%
    B2: 15%
    B3: 12%
    B4: 8%
    Total: 75%.
  Remaining 25% owned by non-blocked persons not modeled.
  No double-counting: each ownership interest in C is counted once.
data.blocked_verdicts: C is BLOCKED under the full-attribution-through-blocked-intermediaries approach (aggregate blocked ownership = 60.6% ≥ 50%). Under multiplicative-through-all, C would NOT be blocked (43.45%).
data.guidance_basis: OFAC 50 Percent Rule (FAQ 398 and related guidance). Same interpretive framework as Cases 2–4. This case adds a second blocked owner (D) and demonstrates convergent paths from two different blocked persons through both blocked and non-blocked intermediaries. The full-attribution approach yields a blocked verdict; multiplicative yields not-blocked. The case also illustrates that the interpretive choice matters even with multiple blocked owners.
data.weakest_point: Again, the precise OFAC treatment of indirect ownership through a majority-owned (blocked) intermediary is the load-bearing rule on which I am least certain: full attribution (counting the intermediary's full downstream ownership as blocked ownership and attributing it to the upstream blocked owner) versus strict multiplication along every path. My computation uses full attribution, which yields C blocked at 60.6%; multiplicative yields 43.45% and not blocked. I am not certain which OFAC has officially prescribed, and this is the central interpretive risk across all cases in this set.

data.case_name: Case 1 — Baseline: all buckets represented, 10% bucket mixed but within tolerance
data.computation:
Zero tolerance bucket:
  Origination charge: CD $1,000.00 ≤ LE $1,000.00 → OK, no increase
  Appraisal fee: CD $500.00 ≤ LE $500.00 → OK
  Credit report fee: CD $50.00 ≤ LE $50.00 → OK
  Zero-tolerance violations: none

10% aggregate bucket:
  Sum of LE amounts = $1,000.00 + $300.00 + $150.00 + $120.00 = $1,570.00
  10% threshold = $1,570.00 × 0.10 = $157.00
  Sum of CD amounts = $1,050.00 + $290.00 + $160.00 + $125.00 = $1,625.00
  Aggregate increase = $1,625.00 − $1,570.00 = $55.00
  Since $55.00 ≤ $157.00, the 10% tolerance is not exceeded → no violation

No-limit bucket:
  Prepaid interest: LE $800.00 → CD $850.00 (increase $50.00); no tolerance limit applies → no cure required
  Homeowner's insurance: LE $600.00 → CD $600.00 → no change

Overall: no bucket exceeds its tolerance; no cure amount owed.
data.violations: None. Zero-tolerance fees unchanged; 10% aggregate increase $55.00 is within the $157.00 threshold; no-limit fees have no tolerance.
data.clause_basis: Zero-tolerance: 12 CFR §1026.19(e)(3)(i) (fees paid to creditor/affiliate or to a provider the creditor requires the borrower to use, where the borrower cannot shop; also transfer taxes). 10% aggregate tolerance: §1026.19(e)(3)(ii) (aggregate of charges for third-party services where the borrower may shop and the creditor does not require a particular provider; the amount in the Closing Disclosure may not exceed the Loan Estimate amount by more than 10% of the sum of those Loan Estimate charges). No tolerance limit: §1026.19(e)(3)(iv) (charges not subject to tolerance, such as prepaid interest, property insurance premiums, escrow account deposits). Cure obligation: §1026.19(e)(3)(iii) (if the 10% tolerance is exceeded, the creditor must pay the excess to the consumer).
data.weakest_point: Bucket assignments rest on whether the borrower can shop and whether the creditor requires a particular provider; I assumed the borrower can shop for title, survey, pest, and recording, and that the creditor selected the appraisal and credit report provider, but the specific facts of a real transaction could change those assignments (e.g., a recording fee could be zero-tolerance if the creditor selected the provider). The dollar amounts are constructed and do not come from a specific published example. The arithmetic is exact as shown.

data.case_name: Case 2 — Mixed directions in 10% bucket; aggregate well within tolerance; illustrates aggregate vs. sum-of-increases distinction
data.computation:
Zero tolerance bucket:
  Origination charge: $1,200.00 = $1,200.00 → OK
  Appraisal fee: $450.00 = $450.00 → OK
  Zero-tolerance violations: none

10% aggregate bucket:
  ΣLE = $900.00 + $350.00 + $200.00 + $100.00 + $250.00 = $1,800.00
  10% threshold = $1,800.00 × 0.10 = $180.00
  ΣCD = $980.00 + $300.00 + $220.00 + $95.00 + $260.00 = $1,855.00
  Aggregate increase = ΣCD − ΣLE = $1,855.00 − $1,800.00 = $55.00
  Since $55.00 ≤ $180.00, the 10% tolerance is not exceeded → no violation

Note on method — the 10% test is an aggregate comparison (ΣCD vs ΣLE), NOT a sum of the individual increases:
  Individual changes: Title +$80, Survey −$50, Pest +$20, Recording −$5, Escrow +$10
  Sum of increases (ignoring decreases) = $80 + $20 + $10 = $110
  Sum of decreases = −$55
  Net change = $55
  Even the incorrect sum-of-increases figure ($110) is below the $180 threshold here, so no violation would be flagged under either approach in this particular case; the distinction matters when the sum of increases would exceed the threshold but the net aggregate does not (see Case 3).

No-limit bucket:
  Prepaid interest: LE $1,000.00 → CD $1,050.00 (increase $50.00); no tolerance limit → no cure
  Homeowner's insurance: no change

Overall: no violation; no cure.
data.violations: None. Zero-tolerance fees unchanged; 10% aggregate increase $55.00 ≤ $180.00 threshold; no-limit fees not subject to tolerance.
data.clause_basis: Zero-tolerance: §1026.19(e)(3)(i). 10% aggregate tolerance: §1026.19(e)(3)(ii) — the rule measures the aggregate amount of the charges in the Closing Disclosure against the aggregate amount in the Loan Estimate, not against a sum of individual increases. No tolerance limit: §1026.19(e)(3)(iv).
data.weakest_point: Bucket assignments depend on whether the borrower could shop and whether the creditor required a particular provider; I assumed shopping was permitted for title, survey, pest, recording, and escrow, and that the creditor selected the appraisal provider. The dollar amounts are constructed. The arithmetic is exact. The key distinction — aggregate vs sum-of-increases — is correctly applied, but in this case both approaches yield no violation, so the case does not by itself demonstrate a wrong result; that is shown in Case 3.

data.case_name: Case 3 — Mixed directions; sum-of-increases would exceed 10% but aggregate does not (illustrates the defect this suite catches)
data.computation:
Zero tolerance bucket:
  Origination charge: $1,000.00 = $1,000.00 → OK
  Appraisal fee: $400.00 = $400.00 → OK
  Zero-tolerance violations: none

10% aggregate bucket (CORRECT method — aggregate vs aggregate):
  ΣLE = $1,000.00 + $400.00 + $200.00 + $100.00 + $300.00 = $2,000.00
  10% threshold = $2,000.00 × 0.10 = $200.00
  ΣCD = $1,250.00 + $300.00 + $180.00 + $95.00 + $350.00 = $2,175.00
  Aggregate increase = ΣCD − ΣLE = $2,175.00 − $2,000.00 = $175.00
  Since $175.00 ≤ $200.00, the 10% tolerance is NOT exceeded → no violation, no cure

INCORRECT method — sum of increases (ignoring decreases):
  Increases: Title +$250.00, Escrow +$50.00 → sum of increases = $300.00
  Decreases: Survey −$100.00, Pest −$20.00, Recording −$5.00 → sum of decreases = −$125.00
  A flawed implementation that compares only the sum of increases ($300.00) to the 10% threshold ($200.00) would (wrongly) conclude a violation and demand a cure of $100.00, even though the correct aggregate method shows no violation.
  This case exists to expose that defect: the rule's text requires the aggregate comparison, and a sum-of-increases approach is the error this suite is designed to catch.

No-limit bucket:
  Prepaid interest: LE $900.00 → CD $950.00 (increase $50.00); no tolerance limit → no cure

Overall: under the correct aggregate method, no violation and no cure; a sum-of-increases implementation would incorrectly flag a violation.
data.violations: Under the correct aggregate method: none. Zero-tolerance fees unchanged; 10% aggregate increase $175.00 ≤ $200.00 threshold; no-limit fee increase not subject to tolerance. A sum-of-increases approach would incorrectly report a 10% violation with a $100.00 cure; that result is the defect this case exposes.
data.clause_basis: Zero-tolerance: §1026.19(e)(3)(i). 10% aggregate tolerance: §1026.19(e)(3)(ii) — the rule compares the aggregate amount of the charges in the Closing Disclosure to the aggregate amount in the Loan Estimate, and the tolerance is 10% of the sum of the Loan Estimate charges; it does not compare each fee individually or sum only the increases. No tolerance limit: §1026.19(e)(3)(iv).
data.weakest_point: Bucket assignments (borrower-can-shop for title, survey, pest, recording, escrow) are assumed; if any of those fees were actually zero-tolerance because the creditor required a particular provider, the analysis and result would change. The numbers are constructed. The aggregate-vs-sum-of-increases distinction is the central point and is correctly drawn, but I am not certain the specific fee amounts match any published example; they are illustrative.

data.case_name: Case 4 — 10% aggregate tolerance violation with cure; mixed directions
data.computation:
Zero tolerance bucket:
  Origination charge: $1,500.00 = $1,500.00 → OK
  Appraisal fee: $400.00 = $400.00 → OK
  Zero-tolerance violations: none

10% aggregate bucket:
  ΣLE = $1,200.00 + $500.00 + $250.00 + $150.00 + $350.00 = $2,450.00
  10% threshold = $2,450.00 × 0.10 = $245.00
  ΣCD = $1,600.00 + $450.00 + $260.00 + $140.00 + $400.00 = $2,850.00
  Aggregate increase = ΣCD − ΣLE = $2,850.00 − $2,450.00 = $400.00
  Amount exceeding the 10% tolerance = $400.00 − $245.00 = $155.00
  → The 10% tolerance is exceeded by $155.00; this is a violation.
  Cure amount owed by creditor to consumer = $155.00

Note on mixed directions:
  Increases: Title +$400.00, Pest +$10.00, Escrow +$50.00 → sum of increases = $460.00
  Decreases: Survey −$50.00, Recording −$10.00 → sum of decreases = −$60.00
  Net change = $400.00
  The correct aggregate method uses the net change ($400.00) against the threshold, not the gross increases. Because the net exceeds the threshold, a cure is required; the decreases do not eliminate the violation but reduce the cure amount.

No-limit bucket:
  Homeowner's insurance: LE $600.00 → CD $620.00 (increase $20.00); no tolerance limit → no cure

Overall: 10% bucket violation; cure = $155.00; zero-tolerance and no-limit buckets have no violations.
data.violations: 10% aggregate bucket: tolerance exceeded by $155.00; cure amount = $155.00 per §1026.19(e)(3)(iii). Zero-tolerance bucket: no violation. No-limit bucket: no violation.
data.clause_basis: Zero-tolerance: §1026.19(e)(3)(i). 10% aggregate tolerance: §1026.19(e)(3)(ii) — the excess over 10% of the sum of the Loan Estimate charges must be cured. Cure obligation: §1026.19(e)(3)(iii). No tolerance limit: §1026.19(e)(3)(iv).
data.weakest_point: Bucket assignments for survey, pest, recording, escrow are based on the assumption that the borrower can shop; if the creditor instead required a particular provider, those fees would move to zero tolerance and the result would change. The dollar amounts are constructed. The arithmetic is exact as shown.

data.case_name: Case 5 — Zero-tolerance violation with cure; 10% bucket flat; no-limit increase
data.computation:
Zero tolerance bucket:
  Origination charge: CD $1,100.00 > LE $1,000.00 → increase of $100.00 → violation of zero tolerance
  Appraisal fee: $400.00 = $400.00 → OK
  Credit report fee: $50.00 = $50.00 → OK
  Zero-tolerance violation: Origination charge increased by $100.00; cure amount = $100.00 (the full increase must be paid by the creditor)

10% aggregate bucket:
  ΣLE = $900.00 (only title insurance in this bucket)
  10% threshold = $900.00 × 0.10 = $90.00
  ΣCD = $900.00 → increase = $0.00 ≤ $90.00 → no violation

No-limit bucket:
  Prepaid interest: LE $800.00 → CD $900.00 (increase $100.00); no tolerance limit → no cure
  Homeowner's insurance: no change

Overall: zero-tolerance violation for origination charge, cure = $100.00; 10% bucket no violation; no-limit bucket no violation.
data.violations: Zero-tolerance bucket: origination charge increased $100.00 → violation; cure amount = $100.00 (creditor must pay the full increase to the consumer). 10% bucket: no violation. No-limit bucket: no violation.
data.clause_basis: Zero-tolerance: §1026.19(e)(3)(i) — origination charge is a fee paid to the creditor, subject to zero tolerance; any increase must be cured in full. Cure obligation: §1026.19(e)(3)(iii) (the creditor must pay the amount of the increase). 10% aggregate tolerance: §1026.19(e)(3)(ii) — no violation here because the aggregate did not increase. No tolerance limit: §1026.19(e)(3)(iv) — prepaid interest is expressly excluded from tolerance and may increase without cure.
data.weakest_point: Origination charge is clearly a zero-tolerance fee under §1026.19(e)(3)(i); I am confident in that assignment. The other assignments (title insurance in 10% bucket, prepaid interest in no-limit bucket) follow the usual treatment. The dollar amounts are constructed. The arithmetic is exact.
